Utilizing scanning tunnelling microscopy, researchers investigated and analyzed the Local Density of States (LDS) of graphene, gold and silicon in various environments. By examining these I-V curves at different points of interest, researchers can uncover unique atomic resonance frequencies, providing insights into the underlying electronic properties. Data collected from graphene, gold and silicon surfaces showcased distinct LDS profiles, characterized by a low-frequency peak at 0.16 eV for graphene, a broad low-frequency shoulder starting at approximately 0.60 eV for gold and a double-peak structure in the LDS of silicon with peaks at 0.40 eV and 0.60 eV. By comparing these findings to established Electronic Density of States (EDOS) profiles, researchers validated that the LDA representation accurately captures the electronic character of each material as initially expected. However, the data also revealed a notable discrepancy between the EDOS and LDS for silicon, suggesting possible resonant tunnelling phenomena, potentially indicating the presence of uninvestigated electronic states. Furthermore, by studying the LDS of graphene and silicon in air and ultra-high vacuum environments, researchers observed no significant variation in the electronic properties, suggesting that air does not impact the resonance frequencies, although it does affect the overall tunnelling current. Finally, by analyzing the LDA representations, researchers can identify and classify defects on the surface, providing quantitative data on the current that falls off as the tunnelling tip moves further away from the defect. By sending the LDA data through a Fourier Transform, researchers can obtain the Frequency Shift versus Displacement, providing insights into the interaction between the tunnelling tip and electronic states. The Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs, comprising over 18,000 theorems, has facilitated significant advancements in theorem verification. Despite its accomplishments, a substantial number of proofs are marred by shortcomings such as ambiguous abbreviations and the absence of clarity in domain definitions. We propose that the Isabelle tool can address these issues by executing a second verification pass on existing proof objects. As a result, the overall quality of proofs can be enhanced, benefiting the entire community. We examined proof objects in the Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs amounting to 13,374 megabytes, thereby demonstrating the feasibility of automatic analysis on a large-scale dataset. We identified numerous instances of poor practice, such as unexplained theorem references and poorly constructed sets, as well as identified core areas requiring improvement, such as existing tools and domain definitions. Furthermore, we present a versatile, adaptable proof verification tool dubbed "framework" that can be easily integrated into Isabelle environments for enhancing existing verification processes. When tested across 1838 directories, our framework identified 7567 theorems requiring domain definition clarification, 7485 theorem references in need of refinement, and 5707 potential set-constraint errors. The "framework" is now available online for public access, allowing the community to contribute and enhance it further. We also discuss potential challenges and present a compelling case as to why the Isabelle tool has the capacity to significantly enhance the quality of existing proof objects, ultimately ushering in a new era of improved theorem-based verification within the Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs. The improved, updated proof objects can be accessed through: https://github.com/joelcm/tuflramework/tree/main/improved-proofs and the original, unimproved proof objects can be accessed through: https://github.com/joelcm/tuflramework/tree/main/original-proofs. With this initiative, our vision is to establish a robust, high-quality archive of formal proofs, thereby ensuring that the Isabelle community continues to build upon this collective knowledge. At the same time, our approach also achieves significant time complexity reductions in these tasks, which is an important finding. The theoretical and experimental investigation of pullin (an effect where light moves at a variance in direction from its incident beam upon interacting with a medium) has gained significant interest in experimental sciences. A comprehensive review of theoretical and experimental studies on pullin was provided in the journal Optics & Laser Technology. Building upon that work, this research presents the first measurement of unusual pullin in a colloidal solution of Nycodan in olive oil. To achieve this, we employed laser beam propagation through the solution and measured the optical pull by observing the change in direction of the beam as it passed through a filter. A perpendicular electric field was applied to the solution to induce unusual pullin by making the refractive index of the parallel index plane anisotropic. Measuring the angle between the beam and the filter allowed us to calculate optical pull by minimizing the error using the method of least squares. A significant pullin angle of 18.6 degrees ±1.6 degrees at 6 volts was observed at 25°C, revealing a linear relationship between pullin angle and applied voltage. Moreover, this research demonstrates the feasibility of measuring unusual pullin by laser beam propagation, offering a novel method for observing pullin in the study of electromagnetic interactions with matter. The effectiveness of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) largely depends on the employed architecture. Research has shown that specific architectures excel in processing graphs of particular sizes by leveraging a concept called break-down. A promising approach, known as transfer learning, allows GNNs to adapt to a new, untrained task by incorporating models trained on similar tasks. However, there's currently limited understanding of its potential on real-world datasets. Our study delves into this by examining the effectiveness of transfer learning in GNNs on various real-world datasets across different scales. We introduce GNNs with a novel break-down property, and experiments reveal that models trained on larger graphs, employing multi-layer architectures, exhibit superior performance on smaller graph datasets. Conversely, reverse transfers also demonstrate comparable results. Through in-depth analysis, we gain insight into the underlying principles, concluding that a diverse model pool and thorough training are crucial for successful transfer learning. Consequently, our work may aid in enhancing the efficiency of model development, training, and deployment for real-world applications. The associated code has been made available on GitHub.

This research proposes a new feature allocation mechanism for suggestion boxes to enhance user engagement in providing feedback suggestions to organizations. To address the low submission rates resulting from users' privacy concerns, we suggest a dual-feature box model. On one hand, the 'Suggestion Box' allows users to submit a range of open-ended suggestions without expectation of implementation. On the other hand, the 'Feedback Box' where users can submit specific comments along with a recommended action expected from the organization. By utilizing a dual box design, we aim to stimulate user participation by safeguarding their anonymity and offering two submission options. Our model preallocates a portion of suggestions to the Feedback Box and aims to maximize the organization's expected utility through a decision-theoretic approach for allocating user-submitted suggestions between the two boxes. Our empirical analysis reveals a significant 70-85% (or higher) submission rate to the Feedback Box and a corresponding 15-30% (or lower) submission rate to the Suggestion Box. Furthermore, our user study with 34 users indicates that 77% of users would be more willing to submit feedback if given the option to select action. In addition, our design has garnered a high level of user satisfaction, and the vast majority of users believe that submitting feedback with an expected action enhances the organization's ability to act upon their feedback. In summary, our dual-feature allocation model for suggestion boxes has achieved enhanced submission rates and improved organization response. It has also been designed with a user-centric approach and incorporates a comprehensive set of user-friendly features. Ultimately, our user study has affirmatively validated our design decisions. This extensive analysis on a relatively large lattice enabled us to make a precise determination of the critical exponents, especially for the magnetization and correlation functions, in three-dimensional Heisenberg spin models. Our results confirm the non-analytic momentum dependence of the spin susceptibility in the paramagnetic phase and provide the critical exponents with high accuracy: $\gamma_m = 2.038(2)$, $\gamma_\xi = 2.02(2)$ and $\nu = 0.02(2)$. We also compared our findings with existing numerical and Monte Carlo results, yielding excellent agreement. Furthermore, we addressed a long-standing debate on the sign versus magnitude critical exponents by showing that the former can be accurately determined, thereby reinforcing the magnitude convention for critical exponents in three-dimensional Heisenberg magnets. Through a generalisation of the spin-dimer model, we were able to systematically analyse the effects of increasing momenta on the spin susceptibility and identify the dominant contributions, revealing a shift in dominance from the two-site to the four-site momentum terms as temperature decreases. This crucial insight enabled us to explain the square-law relationship observed by Henkel and Ballesteros between the integrated momentum-dependent susceptibility and momentum, specifically for the 3D Heisenberg model and certain classical spin models. We were also able to extend this understanding to the 3D Heisenberg model and uncover a broader, more comprehensive universal framework. We were able to determine the universal relationships for $n=2$ and $4$, while revealing that $K_1$ and $n=1$ contributions do not integrate in a universal manner, and that $K_3$ and $n=3$ contributions require further investigation. We were able to derive the universal relationship for $n=5$, while confirming the non-integrable nature of $K_7$ and $K_9$. Predictive computational methods for solving time-varying matrix equations are discussed, with an emphasis on algorithms that use the future state of variables. A framework is proposed for developing and evaluating algorithms of this type, which requires the proposed algorithm to be predictive, meaning its predictions accurately represent the future state of the variables, even when the future is unknown. Many existing methods are found to be non-predictive in nature, which can hinder their performance when working with uncertain or noisy data. As future data is often unavailable, a data-driven approach is typically used to compensate, although this can be circumvented in some cases. A novel method, zeroing neural networks, is proposed, which uses future information to solve problems efficiently, even without relying on a data-driven approach. Furthermore, ZNN is shown to be applicable to a broad range of problems, including linear and nonlinear systems, scalar equations, and higher-order systems. Derivations for these various cases are provided, which are unified by a clear condition for predictivity, highlighting how ZNN is well-suited to handle dynamic systems and has the potential to be adapted for other predictive tasks. With the ability to incorporate noise models, ZNN is shown to be capable of providing time-varying estimates, which are particularly valuable in high-order system applications. From a theoretical perspective, it is found that ZNN is compatible with the concept of ergodicity and is linked to a dynamical map. As ZNN is a nonlinear algorithm, it is expected that applying it to a linear problem will result in slight deviations, which are quantified. Importantly, ZNN is shown to be robust to noise and is suitable for use in systems with time-varying parameters, making it a valuable tool for a wide range of matrix-based applications. Several case studies are presented to demonstrate ZNN's capabilities, starting with the high-dimensional Ising model, which is used to illustrate how ZNN is applicable to equilibrium problems. Next, the algorithm is applied to non-equilibrium problems, including the Ising model with a field and an electron transport problem. Finally, ZNN is shown to be capable of providing time-varying estimates for a nonlinear system, highlighting its potential for use in a variety of practical applications. From a computational perspective, it is found that ZNN is a feasible solution for large problems, as a key condition for predictivity involves the future and not the past. In our tests, the LE model achieved a 94.78% constraint accuracy rate with a 5% confidence threshold, while also demonstrating superior scalability, outperforming traditional screening methods by an order of magnitude. Furthermore, the LE model's integration enabled accurate constraint screening even under extreme weather conditions in 2030, revealing potential limits in machine learning-based screening models without data from future energy scenarios. Utilizing the LE model, we identified viable solutions to power shortages during winter storms in future energy scenarios. By utilizing a combination of interior and exterior images, we develop a unified representation of the car's surface, merging the extrinsic and intrinsic camera parameters to synchronize the views of the same scene. Our novel object representation remains invariant across various camera angles and positions, enabling accurate and robust results in different scenarios. Validation on a diverse set of 33 car models and 2815 input images confirms our method's efficiency and generalizability. Moreover, our proposed method avoids common pitfalls, such as spurious regions and over-reliance on specific reference images, particularly in novel views and unusual camera positions, as demonstrated on images not seen during training and new viewpoints around the same object. To address these challenges, we present two powerful strategies grounded in pure local search, which we've called SUMEET I and II. Our proposed algorithms incorporate innovative component-based reductions, focusing on single-item and item-dropping techniques, and employ a min-max initial selection method. By combining these elements, we've demonstrated the superior performance of SUMEET I and II in generating certified, all-optimal solutions for the Budget Maximum Cover and Set-Union Knapsack Problems. Our experiments showcase the capabilities of our algorithms, with precise solutions found in under a minute for problem instances with up to 1.1 million items across 11 different benchmarks. Notably, our results significantly outperform previous state-of-the-art approaches, including well-tuned heuristics and metaheuristics. To facilitate reproducibility and sharing knowledge, we've created a public GitHub repository containing our code, data, and graphical visualizations. This comprehensive resource serves as an accessible knowledge base, offering a range of related information, including project documentation and pure local search knowledge. Furthermore, our generated solutions, execution times, and solution quality, plotted in Candelain diagrams, are available for sharing and potential use as a baseline benchmark. These innovative tools enable the identification of top-performing solutions, allowing others to leverage our findings, and facilitating a collaborative challenge to find better solutions, known as the "Basin Finding Challenge." To date, our proposed algorithms hold the current best known solutions, and remain the sole known solutions for the 34 publicly available benchmarks, and these results, along with other important information, are recorded in the Basins Repository, a comprehensive database containing our proposed algorithms, their performance, and related knowledge. This database serves as an open platform for collaboration, where other researchers can share their findings, build upon existing knowledge, and engage in a collective pursuit of better solutions. By leveraging these resources, we believe it is feasible to identify and leverage domain-specific reductions, ultimately leading to the discovery of better solutions. A novel method employing Control Barrier Functions has been developed for creating safe and resilient motion planning algorithms capable of adapting to variable robotics environments. The strategy entails designing a global control strategy using an efficient and adaptable meromorphic CBF, which requires an initial trajectory and velocity plan. An online re-planning process is triggered by cBF metrics indicating significant trajectory deviation from desired goals. In addition, a novel cBF-based velocity parameterization is presented, which incorporates robot speed into the meromorphic cBF design. This allows for tighter control and reduced trajectory deviation. Velocity-based design also facilitates cBF stability and robustness analysis, which is demonstrated through both theoretical and simulation data analysis. Furthermore, this approach is showcased in a real-time robotic experiment involving a mobile base platform navigating around dynamic obstacles. Consequently, this method excels in its capacity to adaptively respond to changing environments and achieve safe and efficient navigation. The development of this approach is facilitated by the AIDRA robotic testbed, which provides real-time hardware-in-the-loop testing for assessing robot software and controllers. As such, this framework offers a versatile and adaptable tool for advanced robotics applications. The accompanying code is available on the Git repository https://git.sr.cinvestav.mx/robotics-lab-iciv/main_planning_for_dynamic_envs. https://dx.ros.org/samples.git, which is also the foundation for future extensions to more intricate robotic systems and applications. Future work will involve incorporating predictive models of variable environments, such as those found in changing terrain or wind-swept roads, to develop more robust and adaptive robot systems. The underlying mathematical results presented in this work hold significant independent value and could be extended to a broader array of control challenges. The corresponding mathematicals can be found in the accompanying document https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.13685. For every ring R, we can establish a smallest upper bound for its cardinality by considering the cardinality of each individual set in the family of all sets that form a unimodular ideal within R. We call this bound the 'binding number' of the ring. We examine the binding numbers for various types of rings, particularly commutative rings with 1, and uncountable principal ideal rings, discovering that they all have a binding number equal to or greater than the cardinality of the continuum. We explore the binding numbers for nil rings, and resolve a question regarding the binding number of a commutative ring with 1 by demonstrating that it can be equal to any finite cardinal number. We introduce a related concept known as the 'loosening number' of a set of polynomials, representing a special type of unimodular ideal, and show that it shares many similarities with the binding number, but in the case of a commutative ring with 1, the loosening number can be strictly greater than the binding number. We examine the loosening numbers for several types of rings, including nil rings, and discover that they can take on any cardinality consistent with the underlying binding number, but cannot exceed it. Finally, we consider a more general version of these concepts, applicable to any type of multialgebra, and provide further results in this more encompassing context. A comprehensive list of questions and potential areas of research related to these concepts is also included. Josephine serves as a model for modern programming environments that integrate multiple languages with varying types and lifetimes. Our investigation into Josephine reveals complexities arising from the interactions between Rust's ownership and borrowing rules, TypeScript type system constraints, and JavaScript dynamic typing, resulting in a unique triad of language interoperability challenges. Our analysis demonstrates that Josephine can safely overcome these challenges in a context where a TypeScript reference to a Rust value is transferred to JavaScript, deleted in JavaScript, and subsequently accessed in Rust. Our proof of concept demonstrates that Josephine can safely handle such cases in practice, and a performance benchmark confirms its lightweight implementation. Furthermore, our research highlights additional safety risks associated with cross-language data exchange in web applications that can be effectively mitigated using Josephine, a technique which may prove applicable to a broader range of language integrations beyond Rust, JavaScript, and TypeScript. Recent advancements in belief propagation list decoding have offered a fresh perspective on iterative decoding techniques. This research builds upon those achievements by introducing a novel approach, the polar subcode method, which enhances the polar decoding scheme. This optimization involves generating multiple subcodes through random manipulations, and then applying these subcodes in successive iterations of the belief propagation decoder. We demonstrate the polar subcode method's efficacy using two subcoding techniques, uniform subcoding, and subcoding with erasures. For each case, we present an optimal method for generating polar subcodes that can be decoded via belief propagation. Furthermore, we apply these methods to diverse scenarios involving polar codes with various rates and varying lengths. The results illustrate the polar subcode method's capacity to boost maximum error rates and reduce list sizes in successive iterations. When compared to standard polar decoding, the polar subcode method offers significant improvements, particularly in cases involving polar codes with low rates or extensive lengths. This breakthrough enables us to achieve top-notch performance in these scenarios without compromising list size. The maximum error rates achieved using the polar subcode method are remarkably close to the theoretical limits, with some cases even surpassing these limits due to list size constraints. The polar subcode method's performance is comparable to cutting-edge list decoders developed by Chen et al. and Abadi et al., which utilize diverse non-optimization-based list decoding techniques. One notable advantage of the polar subcode method is its ability to produce dense subcodes that can be fully decoded via belief propagation, resulting in a reduced memory footprint. Importantly, the polar subcode method's error rates remain stable even when decoding complex polar codes requiring numerous iterations to convey critical information. This robustness, combined with minimal computational overhead, positions the polar subcode method as a versatile and efficient approach to iterative decoding. The experimental findings presented here offer valuable insights into the polar subcode method's capabilities and serve as a reliable starting point for further optimization efforts aimed at enhancing its performance and efficiency. Moreover, the polar subcode method's fundamental properties can be leveraged to develop more sophisticated list size reduction strategies, paving the way for future research in this area. Ultimately, the polar subcode method's performance is largely limited by its list size, suggesting significant potential for growth in this area. The polar subcode method's code and experimental data are publicly available and can be employed to develop enhanced iterative decoding techniques, leading to a positive and promising outlook in this domain. We establish that the perturbations of the identity map in the group of volume-preserving diffeomorphisms play a crucial role in controlling the maximum norm. We provide precise estimates for the maximum norm in terms of parameters from the Whitehead integral. We conclude by examining the conditions under which the maximum norm remains bounded for finite > 0.

Moreover, we prove that for small enough > 0, the non-integral values of the maximum norm can be achieved as perturbations of the identity. We introduce a critical value, denoted as $\lambda_0$, for the L^2 norm of the velocity field, and we prove that for non-integral maximum norms below $\lambda_0$, the solutions can be realized as perturbations of the identity. We further establish the connection between the value $\lambda_0$ and the eigenvalue of the stability problem associated with the identity solution. Ultimately, we conclude that the condition of having a non-integral maximum norm corresponds to the existence of a global-in-time solution for a different initial condition in the problem. We've developed a new method to determine if two quantum circuits produce identical outcomes for a given input, in a linear time framework. This method leverageses the concept of congruence from universal quantum computing, and we've adapted it for use on separate quantum circuits, like those employing different topologies or types of quantum measurements. This approach defines a new language, known as EQ[ technologies], that captures the class of problems solvable in linear time, in a probabilistic setting. We've shown EQ[ technologies] contains notable problems, such as checking if a matrix represents a unitary operation, and EQ[ technologies] is contained within the NEXP time complexity class. This new method has significant implications, as it enables the verification of quantum calculations in certain scenarios, once thought to be limited to quadratic complexity by Bell's inequality. The study of exoplanet atmospheres using low-resolution transit spectroscopy has the advantage of being less affected by stellar activity compared to high-resolution methods, making it a more reliable technique for identifying and classifying exoplanet atmospheres. Despite this advantage, low-resolution transit spectroscopy can also be influenced by stellar activity, particularly in the study of H2O atmospheres, due to its broad features. In this study, we assessed the impact of stellar activity on low-resolution transit spectroscopy by using a model of stellar activity to simulate noise in transit spectra, then determining the corresponding signal-to-noise ratios, and ultimately estimating the required spectrographs' resolution for identifying atmospheres of water-rich exoplanets around G-type stars at 3.5 hours orbit distance. Our analysis revealed that, under current technological conditions, a significant number of stars, such as the Sun, experience such high activity levels during observed periods that special high-activity reduction measures are essential, whether through data rejection or activity-affected data analysis, in order to justify the associated expenses in building dedicated instruments, such as the PLATO 2e mission. In order to make these investments worthwhile, we found that developing high-resolution transit spectroscopy techniques can effectively counteract the influence of stellar activity, thereby revealing exoplanet atmospheric features in the presence of high activity levels. Consequently, we found that this could be accomplished with relatively modest enhancements to existing equipment, and that, in fact, the PLATO 2e mission's proposed mid-resolution spectroscopy (20,000), a mid-step between high and low resolution, might be sufficient to achieve this, thereby facilitating the identification of exoplanet atmospheres even in cases where stellar activity poses a challenge. In order to further minimize the impact of stellar activity, we found that certain sophisticated data analysis techniques, such as using "average transit spectra" to represent a "typical" exoplanet atmosphere, could be effective. In conclusion, we found that a combination of technological enhancements, such as high-resolution spectroscopy, moderately enhanced spectrograph resolution, and in-depth data analysis methods, can effectively mitigate the impact of stellar activity on low- and mid-resolution transit spectroscopy, thereby revealing exoplanet atmospheres in cases where such techniques are not employed. The concept of hypersequent rules allows us to address issues within nonvalid logics by introducing new rules that facilitate inference.  In this research, we introduce two types of hypersequent rules – alleviation and contraction rules – that address specific problems associated with structural rules in any given nonvalid logic that satisfies a particular condition. We then examine the impact of these rules on the decidability, complexity, and size of the axiomatic system, while also ensuring the retention of its semantic properties. A detailed analysis is provided for all possible combinations of two particular structural rules in intuitionistic logic. Our study shows that when these rules are used, it either retains the original logic's property or makes the system equivalent to either intuitionistic or classical logic. We provide comprehensive evidence from examples to illustrate when each of these outcomes occur. Furthermore, we provide theoretical justification for our findings by proving them using a particular method and provide an alternative example-based verification of the rules' effectiveness. This research provides a comprehensive understanding into the rules' efficacy in both positive and problematic nonvalid logics. We also provide an alternative presentation of the rules using a particular method that combines different types of rules and uses a particular concept in logic.

The main goal of the Information Retrieval community has long been to extract meaningful patterns from data, a task rivalled in significance by recent advancements in geometric representation learning. Advances in graph-based methods have led to the development of graph neural networks, which leverage graphs as input data. Graphs can effectively model various types of information, including text, by connecting nodes that share similarities. To maintain computational efficiency while handling complex relationships, hyperbolic graph representations have been employed, utilising a compact embedding space to preserve the graph's structural information. However, these methods typically focus on pre-existing graphs rather than dynamic classification tasks. This work integrates hyperbolic representation learning with the Conceptual Cycle, an advanced text representation technique. Through an analysis of the evolution of text embeddings over time, we demonstrate the potential of the hyperbolic Conceptual Cycle to capture and display the growing classification information. To achieve this, we propose HyperExpan, a method for obtaining high-quality hyperbolic embeddings from the Cycle and iteratively updating them to encode increasing classification data. Experimental evaluations reveal that HyperExpan produces more accurate results than existing methods, which are particularly adept at classification tasks, while also being more resistant to noise and resilient across various classification scenarios. Cyber-Physical Systems require robustness to function properly even with unpredictable disturbances. Assessing robustness involves evaluating a design's ability to meet specifications despite system and environment irregularities. We utilize Time-Trace Logic to create a testing framework that accounts for variations in system and environmental conditions, making it possible to measure robustness with a safety margin. This concept is demonstrated using a case study of a vehicle with a nonlinear autopilot system subject to diverse weather conditions. We show that robustness can be estimated, checked, and analyzed within this framework, which we can also employ to assess the robustness of control systems in the presence of multiple conditions. This research provides a foundation for evaluating robustness in Cyber-Physical Systems, focusing on requirements expressed using Temporal Logic specifications. We also discuss the practical implications of our findings, highlighting opportunities for future investigations. 

Key Contributions:
- We introduce a model for assessing robustness in Cyber-Physical Systems, accounting for variations in system and environmental conditions.
- We introduce a concept of robustness along with a corresponding safety margin.
- We demonstrate the practical application of our framework in autopilot systems, path planning, and autonomous vehicle design. 

Future Work:

We introduce a novel class of optimization challenges, referred to as hidden environment problems. In these tasks, a comprehensive network must detect and identify the hidden configuration of an unseen environment, where its internal structure remains inaccessible to view. This classification of problems differs from traditional optimization tasks, such as optimization on a fixed terrain, as a result of the hidden environment's structure and layout. This hidden environment remains inaccessible until discovered through local interactions with 'detectors' placed within the unseen space. Following the proposal of the Halpern-London environment problem, as a mathematical model to study such hidden environments, we present an instance inspired by a real-world task, referred to as the OBSS - optimized within a real substance search, where a hidden lab layout must be discovered through sensors placed within a container of an unknown substance. This OBSS task is shown to be an instance of the optimization challenge of the group of fixed structures, where it shares various properties. Next, we present a theoretical bound for general algorithms applicable to hidden environments, as well as an efficient solution to the OBSS, both of which are achieved using the principles of the coordinate descent technique. Moreover, these algorithms remain efficient even when the hidden environment's structure and layout change over time. Recent advances in NLP for code-mixed text have been promising, particularly with the help of Transformer models. Yet, these models have consistently underperformed when dealing with code-mixed datasets like concreteNLP-2. A major limitation of existing models lies in their failure to account for the positional encodings of individual sublanguages embedded within the code-mixed text. To overcome this, we've developed Transition Point-based Encoding for Transition-focusing Output (PESTO), an enhanced Transformer model incorporating two unique positional encodings. One encodes the relative position of code-mixed words relative to each other, while the other captures the positional information of words from the dominant language. Our proposed PESTO framework has shown remarkable results on the concreteNLP-2 dataset, achieving a significant 2.1% improvement in accuracy compared to the best previous outcome. Furthermore, detailed analysis of PESTO has been provided in a newly published work. For more details, please refer to the paper titled 'Fine-tuning the Fine-tunes: A Deeper Look into the black-box', available on arXiv. Motion planning algorithms for vehicles, especially in variable environments, have a critical constraint: finding a feasible route that avoids collisions with moving objects. To streamline these solutions, researchers utilize static equivalents, replacing dynamic obstacles with fixed boundaries, based on the assumed trajectory of obstacles. This approach, known as spatial limitation, empowers planners to resolve the issue using simpler, heuristic-based methods. Nevertheless, there's a problem with this strategy - it's not always based on an in-depth analysis of all possible paths. We investigate the possibility of discovering such spatial limitations for particular dynamic planning problems and demonstrate that we've devised an efficient method to find suitable limitations with guaranteed optimal results. We've also developed another method which can suggest spatial limitations that yield improved outcomes. To showcase the value of our work, we've used simplified examples involving straight-line and curved paths. These test cases highlight the benefits of our research and how it can be applied. This paper was originally published as "Spatial Limitation Creation for Motion Planning in Dynamic Settings" in IJCAI '21. The three-dimensional, incompressible Navier-Stokes equations face controversy in their ability to withstand small perturbations of large solutions. Specifically, when these perturbations are large in certain spaces yet mild in intensity, the outcome remains unclear. In this study, we investigate the hypothesis that these perturbations lead to a collapse of the solution in certain spaces. Focusing on steady flows, we demonstrate that when the perturbed solution reaches critical thresholds in spaces like BSV space, the solution will indeed break apart, indicating that these spaces represent a critical capacity in measuring the endurance of the equations to mild perturbations. Our findings expand on previous work by Lechner, Planchon, and Zhang who examined the stability of steady solutions in 2D and extended to 3D. Notably, studying three-dimensional flows proves significantly more demanding due to an absence of useful interpolation estimates in low-regularity settings found in three dimensions. We successfully overcome this limitation by developing a novel method that incorporates a critical combination of high-regularity velocity estimates in scale of micro and non-linear paradigms. Our work now places the three-dimensional findings on a solid analytical foundation, similar to recent two-dimensional results obtained by Zhang. Further research should seek to explore these steady findings in their dynamic counterpart. However, navigating this exploration will necessitate overcoming significant new obstacles.

We develop a theoretical approach to examine the behavior of magnons in antiferromagnetic insulators under intense magnetic fields that are sufficient to cause magnon-magnon interactions. This interaction results in a phenomenon where the magnon distribution becomes displaced towards higher energy states, accompanied by a significant change in the system's effective sublattice imbalance. Our research demonstrates that the magnitude of the displacement is independent of the initial magnetic field's sublattice splitting. Furthermore, we investigate how the magnon distribution changes as the magnetic field is intensified and predict a sudden, first-order transition in the magnon distribution's displacement at a critical field strength. At this critical point, the magnon distribution exhibits a double-humped structure, characterized by minimal interaction at intermediate field strengths. Additionally, we explore the effect of the magnetic field's intensity on the system's effective sublattice imbalance and anticipate a sudden, drastic change in this imbalance at the critical field strength, which should be observable through NMR resonance measurements. Our theoretical findings suggest that magnetic systems where a high-velocity spin rotation can occur in spite of a small, easily manipulated sublattice imbalance may serve as ideal settings for studying the previously discussed phenomena and may yield valuable insights into the physics of materials that are capable of spin-rotation symmetry breaking. One such example of a material that meets these requirements is La$_2$CuO$_4$. Our research predicts that the magnon distribution in La$_2$CuO_4$ exhibits a significant change in response to intense magnetic fields, resulting in a double-humped structure at the critical field strength of approximately 35 debye. This effect should be observable through NMR resonance measurements that utilize the $^{17}$O ion, as the ion is located on a symmetric site within the system. We anticipate that the predicted phenomena and methods of investigation that we have outlined in this study could serve to stimulate significant advancements in the understanding of magnetic field-driven phase transitions in systems where a high-velocity spin rotation can occur. This research introduces two modifications for enhancing the security of Loidreau's code-based cryptosystem.
Originally built on Goppa codes with a specific form of parity-check matrices, the system can be breached in at most q^d operations. By switching to Goppa codes with arbitrary parity-check matrices, the system becomes more resistant to generic attacks. It is proven that the minimum distance between the received message and the information matrix increases at least to d + 1 when a random parity-check matrix is used, which results in a minimum distance of n - d when a systematic generator matrix is used. As a result, the system can resist attacks in at most q^(n - 1) attempts. Furthermore, the system's security can be increased by combining multiple Goppa codes with varying lengths, which results in a system that can resist attacks in at most q^(d_1 +... + d_k) attempts, where n = d_1 +... + d_k. This hybrid system retains a similar message length and key size to the original one, yet offers significantly improved security with a system resistance to attacks in at most q^(n - 1) attempts. The proposed alterations result in significant security enhancements for Loidreau's code-based cryptosystem, which was previously vulnerable to attacks in at most q^d attempts. The new variations have been thoroughly tested using numerical data, which confirms that they are both effective and practical in increasing the system's security. The data reveals that the system's security can be increased by up to 2k bits when a combination of k Goppa codes of equal length n/k is used, which suggests that the proposed alterations are both secure and reliable in increasing the system's security. In vertical Federated Learning, participants typically cannot combine their data due to confidentiality constraints. Learning occurs through iterative cycles of data exchange between participants and a central server, where the server adjusts parameters after receiving new data for each iteration. This study reveals two unforeseen, easy-to-implement attacks on Federated Learning systems. The first attack targets model parameter exchange, where the server broadcasts falsified parameters to several participants at random in each iteration. The greater number of affected participants in an attack cycle increases the risk, where risk is calculated as the product of two factors: the probability of being selected in an attack cycle and the number of selected participants. The server adjusts the model using only the falsified parameters from selected participants. Participants remain unaware of the attack as they receive updates based on their local training and the server's updated model parameters. The second attack involves biased data selection, where the server chooses participants for the next iteration based on the participation in an attack cycle. The server trains the model using only the falsified parameters from selected participants. The first attack reduces the model's accuracy on participant data after an attack cycle, whereas the second attack causes the model to inaccurately predict the class labels on participant data and also alters the class balance in participant data. Both attacks exploit the trust placed by the Federated Learning framework in the server and participants. They are simple to execute as they do not require access to training data or model source code, or manipulation of model parameters on participant side. They are resilient to common data privacy defenses. They are detected on participant data and server data, and even when undetected, they are costly for the server as they require additional iterations to recover. The server and participants can recover from the first attack by verifying the model parameters and participant labels before model updates. The second attack can be recovered from by adding data validation on server data. The recovery methods do not prevent the first attack, where the server loses potential learners in each attack cycle. Document ranking has become an essential component of modern search engines, emphasizing the practical application of learning-based methods in this field. Despite their utility, learning-based methods can be vulnerable to degradation when exposed to noisy labels obtained from crowdsourcing or real-user feedback. To reduce traffic congestion, researchers have been exploring linked automated vehicle platooning as a potential solution. However, establishing these platoons while ensuring the safety of vehicles within them poses a complex challenge. We present a novel method of vehicle platooinformation, which utilizes differential games to create a control strategy for automating linked vehicle platoons. By applying differential games, we break down the control problem into simpler sub-problems and propose an online optimization approach that resolves each part efficiently. Additionally, our approach allows the control problem to be reformulated as a linear system, enabling a straightforward and online-computable solution and thus making it suitable for real-time applications. We back up our theoretical analysis with comprehensive numerical simulations, which demonstrate our approach's performance. Moreover, we test our approach on the USDOT platooning test track to verify its effectiveness. Overall, our research focuses on developing a practical control strategy for automating linked vehicle platoons, which has significant potential for real-world applications. The proposed approach's performance is validated through a combination of analysis, simulation, and experimental testing. These results indicate that our approach is a practical solution to the complex challenge of vehicle platooinformation. By controlling the vehicles' acceleration and reaction parameters, our approach enables safe and stable vehicle platooinformation. Extensive numerical simulations reveal that our approach's stability is unaffected by various parameters such as the communication delay, the number of vehicles, and the simulation time, provided that the vehicles' relative positions and accelerations are known to the leading vehicle. Moreover, our experimental testing of our approach on the USDOT platooning test track shows promising performance, which outperforms existing methods in terms of stability, safety, and online computability, with a remarkable 91.5% to 100% improvement. Overall, our research offers a promising solution to the challenge of vehicle platooinformation. Machine learning models that efficiently use computational resources are highly valued by data scientists and engineers.  Particularly, logistic regression is a popular choice for binary classification tasks due to its balance of accuracy, computational efficiency, and ease of implementation.  Interactive approaches, such as gradient descent, have historically been necessary for taking advantage of the computational efficiency of logistic regression.  We've developed a logistic regression solver, called 'LQR', which employs interior point methods and doesn't require user interaction.  This solver is particularly well-suited for large datasets that fit completely in RAM.  When paired with the correct hyperparameters, LQR is capable of achieving high accuracy at a significantly faster rate than current optimisation methods.  Our research compares the performance of LQR against other optimisation methods and showcases its capabilities through a range of educational jupyter notebooks, available on github.  These notebooks include training LQR on the entire US census dataset and using it to predict whether a person has a high school diploma based on demographic information and other factors.  This project is being released as open-source, open-community licensed software, and is available to download for free.  We believe that LQR is a valuable contribution to the machine learning and optimisation communities and look forward to hearing about any further developments or collaborations.  In addition, we've developed a set of research tools for working with large US census datasets and plan to release several more machine learning and optimisation contributions in the near future.  This project is being primarily developed and maintained by Alex Broad and Anthony Zimmons.  If you're interested in getting in touch or would like to contribute to the project please don't hesitate to contact us.  A key project assumption and guideline for collaboration is that large datasets can be obtained for free through official government websites.  A major project goal and ambition is to expand the scope of available datasets to include other government and publicly available datasets, such as those available from data.gov and to release these datasets in a manner that is compatible with the data.gov API.  This project is being developed as part of the Data66 research initiative and is being supported by the Data66 community.  For more information on the project please see the project github repository and look forward to hearing from you soon.  A collaborative and community-driven approach and effort is highly valued and encouraged.  If you're interested in working with large US census datasets and getting involved in the machine learning and optimisation communities we'd be delighted to hear from you and hear your thoughts and ideas. The growing necessity for online content in the present social environment has sparked a surge in web-based content sharing platforms. Presently, individuals can easily access various social media or content-sharing websites to express their thoughts and connect with others. However, the proliferation of new content has also led to concerns over its impact on the environment, as an enormous amount of unnecessary and often duplicate content is being published. Despite the potential drawbacks, there are also opportunities for positive social and cultural growth, such as promoting empathy and understanding through online storytelling. In this study, we will  a) investigate the motivations and obstacles associated with creating online content, b) examine the ways in which content creators can engage with one another, c) explore the ways in which online communities can incite creative action, and d) highlight best practices for promoting a culture of online content sharing. In addition, we will also delve into the environmental and economic consequences of widespread content creation and present potential solutions to mitigate these negative consequences. Ultimately, this study aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the complex interplay between online content sharing and its far-reaching societal and environmental impacts. It is our hope that this research will inspire future investigations into the various facets of online content creation and its numerous benefits. Furthermore, we also aim to provide insights that can be directly applied by content creators, developers, and policymakers to positively influence this rapidly evolving cultural and technological landscape. In this study, we will focus on social media and content-sharing platforms, such as YouTube, TikTok, Twitter, and Reddit. In clinical trials for Alzheimer's and progressive diseases tracked with continuous data, the mean difference in progress between groups can be distorted due to the varying rates at which patients deteriorate. Accounting for these individual differences is crucial in accurately understanding treatment effects and establishing meaningful thresholds for statistical analysis. A method of analysis that acknowledges and utilizes this variability is known as the natural cubic spline (NCS) approach. In this context, NCS analysis involves creating a smooth curve to represent each patient's disease progression, with key differences in progression evaluated and compared between treatment groups. This comparative method can be particularly useful in identifying key time points where patients' rates of decline differ in response to treatment. To illustrate its utility, NCS analysis is applied to data from a real-world trial examining the effects of lanabecept in patients with Alzheimer's disease. Additionally, steps are provided for incorporating NCS analysis into statistical analysis and how it can be used in conjunction with parametric methods such as repeated measures to provide a more comprehensive understanding of treatment effects. As NCS analysis does not rely on distributional assumptions, it offers an alternative, non-parametric method for examining time-based data and identifying data-driven time points of interest. Importantly, including NCS analysis in a comprehensive approach allows for the detection of treatment-induced differences in patients' rates of decline, providing valuable insights that might have been missed through traditional repeated measures or last-observation-carried-forward analyses. A simulation study demonstrates that combining NCS and repeated measures analyses offers improved statistical power in detecting treatment effects, making it a promising and effective analytical strategy for examining time-based data and identifying meaningful, data-driven time points for further research. Analysis indicates that the combination of these methods is well-capable of detecting non-linear and variable treatment effects, making it an excellent option for analyzing data in Alzheimer's clinical trials, particularly those seeking to identify key time points where patients' rates of decline differ in response to treatment. This method could be widely applied in similar trials involving continuous data and covariate adjustment to help better understand treatment effects. By utilizing NCS and repeating measures analyses, researchers and analysts can gain a deeper, more comprehensive understanding of treatment effects in Alzheimer's disease and related fields. Results show that this basic approach rivals more complex methods that employ pre-trained models and even outperforms some of them in the key metric of class accumulation. Importantly, this finding questions the need for elaborate methods like rehearsal, memory augmentation, and neural network design modifications in combination with pre-trained models and suggests that simple approaches can achieve good results. We demonstrate this on key continual learning settings and datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/andreabanci/PreTrained-Continual-Learning. Building upon this work, we also explore ways to simplify even further the continual learning approach, leveraging a single, small transformer model that is trained sequentially on all the datasets in a 'once-through' process. This basic approach achieves competitive results with large, powerful models that are typically used in continual learning setups. Our work highlights that simple methods, such as the 'once-through' approach, can achieve good results and encourages the research community to look for more efficient solutions to continual learning problems. We also release the code at https://github.com/andreabanci/Simply-Continual-Learning. A demonstration of the 'once-through' approach can be found at https://dreberber.github.io/once-through/. Our goal is to simplify the continual learning approach to better reflect the state-of-the-art methods that are often undistinguishable from the example case at https://dreberber.github.io/once-through/.

High-energy nuclear collisions result in complex many-body systems that integral parts of these systems integrate the Quantum ChromoDynamics (QCD) medium with unique properties. It is essential to understand how this medium impacts the formation of the collision system, its collision structure, and how it reflects the characteristics of the QCD medium. To address these questions, novel instruments are needed that can analyze the three-dimensional flow of particles produced in collisions. 

This article will review three-dimensional flow analysis, covering its underlying physics, measurement approaches, and related theoretical comprehension. We also will discuss how this analysis can provide insights into the collision structure and how it is connected to the QCD medium's Equation-of-State (EOS). 

In addition to reviewing 3-dimensional flow, this article will explore further instruments, such as the using leading particles for a detailed system investigation. Leading particles are produced early in the collision process, providing valuable information to understand the collision system. 

Ultimately, this article will explore and discuss how 3-dimensional flow analysis and other investigative methods can be merged to study the collision structure and to probe the properties of the QCD medium.

Graph neural networks (GNNs), which extend CNNs to learn graph structures, are applied in various tasks. As GNNs have a smaller number of parameters than CNNs, they offer enhanced generalization capabilities and better resistance to attacks. This research considers using GNNs in wireless communication systems, specifically in graph-based channel estimation and message recognition. A decentralized channel estimation approach based on GNNs is proposed, using an orthogonal frequency division multiplexing system as an example. With this method, local devices can generate structured features and exchange them to improve inference results through a GNN. Results indicate that this approach can achieve a 94.1% accuracy in channel estimation. Furthermore, it compares the performance of GNNs, CNNs, and traditional methods in various settings, showing that GNNs outperforms others in some cases. Additionally, a GNN-based message recognition system is studied, demonstrating its potential to achieve a 97.2% classification accuracy. Overall, the research introduces the application of GNNs in wireless communication systems and evaluates their efficiency in graph-based message recognition and channel estimation. The results illustrate the benefits and potential of GNNs in these tasks. Future research opportunities are also discussed.

The primary goal of model compression is to reduce the resource-intensive nature of trained deep learning models while maintaining their accuracy. A popular approach to achieving this involves using a smaller, lean model to approximate the behavior of a larger model. However, model compression faces challenges when it comes to preserving the larger model's outputs, particularly in complex tasks such as image recognition. To mitigate this issue, research has developed knowledge distillation as a method to enable a smaller model to learn the larger model's class probabilities. Although successful, knowledge distillation often requires multiple iterations to converge, which can be time-consuming and inefficient. To address this limitation, researchers have developed InDistill, a distillation method that preserves data flow and has been implemented in PyTorch. According to experimental findings, InDistill achieves comparable results for a set of lean models compressing a ResNet-50 image classifier on the CIFAR10 and ImageNet datasets, using a significantly reduced number of iterations, in addition to demonstrating improved data flow preservation. To validate the effectiveness of InDistill, researchers have conducted a series of studies that demonstrate its ability to preserve data flow and other models' knowledge when distilling them. Notably, InDistill has successfully compressed the DenseNet169 model, retaining the full accuracy of the larger model. Deep learning pre-training, particularly popular for semantic segmentation, typically relies on choosing between object detection and semantic segmentation tasks for initial pre-training. We support the idea that utilizing monocular depth prediction for pre-training can yield better results, but our research focuses on its broader implications. We analyzed various levels of integration, including scikit-image's auto estimate functions and high-performance methods like DeepStereo and Sparse-to-Dense, as well as different methods of loss function, input, and output. Our findings indicate that depth estimates from low-performance or non-optimal methods are ineffective for pre-training and only high-quality outputs, such as normals or weights, provide benefits. Surprisingly, using S4 with a novel softmax output outperformed other methods, but regular loss function for this type of problem didn't work as expected. With an adapted cross-entropy loss function, S4 produced scene-wise scores on CamResta, rising from 91.5 to 92.9. Similarly, using standard or 1+2 channel configurations for monocular and multiview inputs on KITTI, IAQ+SPair with standard configurations scored 83.7, 83.5, 82.9 for monocular, semilabeled monocular, and semilabeled multiview inputs. A distinguishing aspect of our approach is the rigorous mathematical framework for choosing the pivot element and pivot row that surpasses the efficiency of Pseudo-Reverse-Feasibility, which previously held this standard. We've also established a comprehensive list of possible AP pivot techniques, and certain methods can be viewed as variants of the El Gamal Karmarkar algorithm or as enhanced versions of the simplex method's slack pivot. Building upon this foundation, we've devised new AP pivot-based algorithms with iteration limits, and when paired with AP pivot choices 4 or 6, these algorithms exhibit a maximum number of iterations proportional to n, where n is the number of variables. This marks the first time an AP pivot-based algorithm has achieved an iteration limit proportional to n, surpassing the performance of the AP pivot-El Gamal Karmarkar algorithm. We've also demonstrated the possibility of achieving a linear iteration limit under even more constrained conditions, paving the way for future research. A significant innovation of our work is the development of AP pivot-based algorithms with iteration limits, and we believe that future improvements should prioritize a linear iteration limit under all circumstances. Existing methodologies often impose restrictive prior assumptions or use discriminative models, which fail to provide comprehensive solutions. To address this challenge, a Kernel Mixture Model (KMM) is proposed, which combines multiple kernels with weighted averaging to accurately capture the diversity of natural images. By representing the degraded image as a mixture of clear images, KMM creates an energy function that reflects the degeneration process. A sparse regression module is then developed to compute the clear image, drawing inspiration from the sparse prior assumption of image representation. To efficiently handle non-Gaussian noise, a module that models the noise covariance is added, reformulating the optimization problem in a closed form to obtain the optimal estimate of the clear image. The proposed KMM energy function is shown to effectively account for image sparsity and non-Gaussian noise. To demonstrate its robustness, the method is tested on various challenging scenarios, including the simulation of real blur and noise deblurring problems. We introduce a novel model for dust properties and behavior in the interstellar medium.  It accurately predicts the attenuation of light, the emission spectra of light, and the polarization of light across a broad range of wavelengths and dust densities.  Our model relies on the combination of two types of dust: the astrodust component, comprised of large, complex particles, and a PAH component, comprised of smaller, carbon-based particles.  In regions with low dust densities, the astrodust component dominates, and in regions with high dust densities, the PAH component dominates.  A unique aspect of the astrodust component is that it exhibits polarization in ways that are not linear, which may be related to the presence of massive dust structures.  Our model also relies on the concept of'snowballs', which are areas where the astrodust and PAH components coexist.  By using this approach, our model is able to account for the observed polarization in the Milky Way in ways that align with existing astrophysical observations and predictions, while also identifying potential areas of research and observation.  Specifically, our model suggests that the polarization in the diffuse interstellar medium should be more pronounced at infrared wavelengths, and that the polarization in circumstellar environments should be more common than expected in cases where the scattering optical depth exceeds 0.1.  Overall, our model represents a major step forward in the understanding of the role of dust in the interstellar medium across a wide range of conditions and scales.  In particular, our model highlights the need to develop a new unified theory of dust that can accurately capture the complex distribution of dust in various environments and regions, which may vary from sparse to dense and in the type of dust grains present. The popular "Lights Out" game is explored in detail, focusing on a variant with infinite grids known as LOGI.  The concept of a "click" on an infinite grid cell is introduced, where a click affects neighboring cells and reduces their values by one, with a subset of cells known as "dead ends" having no adjacent active neighbors.  A dead end click is deemed valid if it can activate an infinite number of adjacent cells.  The LOGI game is won by extinguishing all active cells except those from dead ends, which can be achieved through specific strategies - initially extinguishing all, or clicking only dead ends, or a combination of both.  The notion of a "clicking force" is developed, where the capacity of a cell set to generate infinite clicks is considered.  The winning strategy involves enabling a "maximum clicks" dilemma where all cells can be extinguished except those from dead ends, and a specific maximum clicks force can be determined for the empty set.  A LOGI game with a finite grid known as LOGN is also examined, focusing on a variant known as LOGN$_m,n$.  The LOGN$_m,n$ game has grid dimensions $m$ rows and $n$ columns, and it's demonstrated that a specific LOGN$_m,n$ game can be solved with a winning strategy if and only if a certain LOGI game has a maximum clicks dilemma.  A mathematical expression for calculating the maximum clicks force of a cell set in LOGI is developed, and used to determine the maximum clicks force of several specific cell sets in LOGI and LOGN$_m,n$.  The research also includes the creation of a computer program named "Lights Out" that is capable of solving LOGI games, as well as playing LOGN$_m,n$ games.  The solutions to the LOGI games involve analyzing the game using a combination of mathematical and computational techniques.  A description of the program's algorithms used to solve LOGI games and play LOGN$_m,n$ games is provided.  The research concludes by asking a question about LOGI games that remain unsolved.  The goal of the research is to gain a deeper understanding of the LOGI game, and to inspire further research into this topic.  A list of the LOGI games solved by the program is included in the appendix. Review-based product recommendation is a crucial component of e-commerce, where the quality of the review information directly affects the effectiveness of such systems. Although current methods have made significant progress in learning review representations, they often fall short by ignoring the diverse perspectives expressed in reviews or the complex interactions between review content and user preferences. To address these limitations, this paper introduces the Sentiment-sensitive Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN) that learns review representations more accurately by incorporating user preferences and varying review sentiments in a interactive learning framework. SIFN allows for interactive learning and sentiment-sensitive representation construction through the incorporation of a) a Sentiment-sensitive Interactive Attention Mechanism (SIAM) for fusing reviews written in different languages or containing diverse sentiment information; and b) a Preference-based Interactive Learning Mechanism (PILM) for learning review representations in an iterative and interactive manner, taking into account user preferences and review sentiment for representation construction. Experiments conducted on three real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of SIFN, showing performance improvements over Strong Baselines, with validation and fairness studies further confirming the sensitivity and fairness of SIFN. Its interface is also compatible with the up-to-date, revised version of power converter design guidelines. Lastly, this model can easily be incorporated into the proposed, general purpose power converter simulation framework. The provided model, files, and support are intended to facilitate the design, simulation, and optimization of analytical converters.

Lie 2-algebras serve as a natural 2-extension of simple Lie algebras and their derivations. They possess a natural intrinsic derivation algebra, which makes them suitable for categorification. Skew-symmetric braided Lie algebras, which arise from the bialgebra structure of a quantum group's infinitesimal Hopb-algebra, are used to construct Lie 2-algebras. Some key Lie 2-algebras are derived from the bialgebra structure of a quantum plane's infinitesimal Hopb-algebra and the adjoint representation of a simple Lie algebra. The paper aims to provide an in-depth review of the construction of these Lie 2-algebras, their properties, and connections to related topics. It will specifically focus on homotopy Lie 2-algebras and their derivation algebra, while dismissing other types of 2-algebra constructions that are not relevant to the topic. The survey will also cover the intrinsic derivation algebra's characteristics, the commutator ideal, and its connections to cohomology in degree one. It will introduce the 2-algebra Lie 2-algebra itself, which is derived from the skew-symmetric braided Lie algebra's natural Lie 2-algebra structure, and its significant properties. The paper will cover Lie 2-algebra cohomology and its connections to the 2-algebra itself, as well as Lie 2-algebra extensions and their relationships to simple Lie algebras and their derivations. It will explore the unique characteristics of cohomology in degree one and the role of adjoint representations in Lie 2-algebra constructions. The growing importance of remote-sensing vector magnetic field (VMF) observations for solar research demands efficient data sharing and dissemination to support a wider community of astronomers. Remote sensing of the sun's surface VMF is limited to inferred data due to the current state of technology. These inferred data, obtained through image reconstruction techniques, often contain noise and biases. Since existing formats only provide the VMF vector itself, along with accompanying error margins, the effect of potential biases is typically overlooked. In order to rectify this, we introduce an approach to flag and document these biases for remote-sensing VMF data. By representing the VMF flux tube definition using an RDF schema, our methodology enables the explicit labeling of biases through RDF annotations. This process is applied to SDO/HMI data, employing a conversion pipeline and specifying not only the employed inversion techniques but also their inherent biases. By documenting these biases, data repositories can maintain transparency in their datasets, comply with Open Data principles, and facilitate the explicit description of biases during data retrieval. Furthermore, this allows the curation of biases within datasets, thereby enhancing data quality and making shared datasets more reliable for solar VMF research. Ultimately, this results in the generation of bias-free inferred VMF data, produced either by removing previously documented biases or by including multiple datasets to mitigate their average impact. In this study, we showcase the effectiveness of our proposed RDF schema and annotation technique using SDO/HMI data, demonstrating its ability to accurately replicate known VMF flux tube biases. Additionally, by applying this method to four active regions, we successfully remove or reduce the bias in their corresponding VMF maps. These findings not only validate the employed approach but also provide valuable insights for solar VMF inversion techniques, ultimately leading to the development of a web-based platform, the Remote-Sensing VMF Bias Alleviation Tool (RSVMF-BAT), for downloading bias-free VMF data, along with matched-pair comparisons of biased and de-biased datasets and corresponding statistical analyses. By using this tool on the VMF@ESO dataset repository, researchers can access a comprehensive dataset of de-biased remote-sensing VMF data, complemented by in-depth statistical results and plots. Consequently, the dissemination of bias-free VMF data supports an increased research throughput, ultimately contributing to a more detailed understanding of the underlying solar physics. Identifying the locations of incidents such as accidents, congestion, and construction is vital for determining their scale, nature, and cause, and is thus crucial for various city planning and decision-making purposes. Although micro-blogging services like Twitter provide real-time updates with detailed geospatial and temporal information, and contain user-generated content including blog and image posts, research on utilizing this data for incident identification is still limited. A novel fusion technique that integrates human and automated processing is also proposed to analyze complex incident patterns, including single-incident threads and multiple-incident discussions. Experimental validation on two datasets, one concerning a plane crash and another with Miami traffic, showed the proposed algorithm's efficiency and effectiveness, and demonstrated its ability to accurately detect incidents mentioned in diverse contexts. Furthermore, the results revealed that human processing aided by AI could enhance data accuracy and provide more reliable incident descriptions and evidence. In general, the research showed that combining computational and human analysis over social media could effectively detect incidents such as plane crashes and congested roads. Future studies could involve investigating other computational methods for extracting incident patterns from large datasets, and using human validation to confirm AI-generated results to reduce errors. A related system prototype, called SPIDER - Instant Incident Identification (III), was also developed and is available for public use. A future extension of this work could involve integrating III with other city decision-making systems and utilizing it for various city planning and decision-making purposes. As data mining and machine learning algorithms become more ubiquitous in practical applications, users with limited technical background are expected to understand and evaluate these algorithms without specialized training. This growing disparity presents a significant challenge, as users with no expertise in programming or machine learning are increasingly expected to deploy these algorithms. Consequently, users are likely to struggle understanding these algorithms, which in turn hampers their ability to trust and interpret the results. This work aims to bridge this gap by proposing a measure to assess the interpretability of algorithms from a human-learning perspective. By adopting a modular approach to learning, we establish that algorithmic interpretability is influenced by two key factors: understanding modular structures and handling exceptions. To gauge the learning difficulties associated with these factors, we develop a comprehensive score that reflects the intricacy of cognitive processes involved in learning these algorithms. This score is utilized to evaluate and compare the interpretability of several algorithms on the datasets from the 2017 UAI Challenge. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of our proposed framework through a survey, which yields surprising results: despite being less accurate, Linear Correlation-based algorithms are preferred over gradient-boosting algorithms such as LightGBM, XGBoost, and Catboost. Building upon this insight, we investigate situations where users tend to favor Linear Correlation-based algorithms over more sophisticated alternatives. Ultimately, we discuss the practical implications of our proposed framework and offer recommendations for enhancing algorithmic interpretability. Specifically, we advise algorithm designers to clarify modular structures and anticipate potential exceptions to make algorithms more intuitive for users to comprehend and identify exceptions that can be readily anticipated. Moreover, we suggest that developers provide users with relevant context, illustrations of modular structures, and example exceptions to facilitate learning and understanding these algorithms. A novel method for Bayesian analysis of extreme events is proposed, incorporating recent advancements in extreme value theory. By viewing event occurrences through a Poisson process and applying extreme value theory via a generalized Pareto distribution, the sample size and rate parameter can be modeled as a negative binomial and phi-distributed variables, respectively. This setup enables estimation via two positive Lyapunov-type inequalities for the mean and variance of the weighted negative binomial distribution's sample size. Building upon this, a Markov-Chain Monte-Carlo algorithm is developed to estimate the parameters, leveraging their geometric mean and pseudo-marginal methods for efficiency. This approach is demonstrated to yield reliable estimators for the scale and location parameters, as well as the return period and extreme value threshold, especially under heavy-tailed scenarios. Its superior performance is empirically validated through comparisons with traditional maximum likelihood estimation and other methods, including those based on transform-downweight techniques, particularly in heavy-tailed scenarios. Additionally, the method exhibits a significant computational speed advantage. Analytical grounds are also provided for the newly proposed estimation algorithms for the threshold and return period. Simulated case studies highlight the method's effectiveness, including its ability to handle complex scenarios with multiple extreme patterns. Last but not least, real-world data are analyzed to showcase the effectiveness of the proposed technique. After reviewing and refining the method, a related R package called 'BAYESXMLE' is developed to implement the proposed approach. The source code is publicly available at the following repository: 'BAYESXMLE'. The proposed estimation algorithms are theoretically and experimentally evaluated for their performance and reliability. Analysis of real-world data using these methods may uncover new insights into extreme events.
