A type of model known as a surrogate model helps to approximate the behavior of a computational model, typically by producing predictions that are quick and accurate when given specific inputs. In the case of wind turbines specifically installed onshore or offshore, these models play a significant role in enabling an efficient design process. This process involves initially running expensive simulations to generate data on load conditions, which is then used to train a more efficient surrogate model. Once the surrogate model is trained, it facilitates the rapid evaluation of various design options without the need for costly simulations, thus enabling an agile design workflow. 

In this study, a statistical assessment of the error associated with using surrogate models in the specific context of wind turbines installed offshore is presented. A multi-stage approach to surrogate modeling that takes into account the non-stationarity of spatial data on wind turbulence and applies a Gaussian process regression chain is demonstrated. The analysis reveals that the error associated with these models, which are trained using data on load conditions generated by the software for 18 specific wind turbines installed offshore, follows a logarithmic distribution. 

A key finding of the study is that incorporating the rapid rotation of wind turbines into the analysis leads to significantly reduced error, with a 50-fold improvement on average in some cases. Additionally, the study finds that incorporating the slow rotation of wind turbines into the analysis leads to a 10-fold improvement in some cases. These results imply that incorporating the effects of rotation at multiple scales into the analysis causes the error associated with these models to significantly undershoot their actual values, thus necessitating the use of error models informed by theoretical distributions such as the chi-square and the t-distribution in order to accurately account for the behavior of these models. The study presents a method for training such error models and finds that the specific error models trained in this study effectively predict the behavior of more efficient models trained in the specific context of wind turbines specifically installed onshore or offshore. 

A potential limitation of the study is that the specific error models presented in this study may not be effective at modeling the behavior of other types of computational models, thus highlighting the need for further research into the behavior of these models. The study further identifies areas for future research into the development of more efficient models trained in the specific context of wind turbines specifically installed onshore or offshore. Deducing the evolution of molecular dynamics from time-resolved experimental data can be challenging, particularly in complex scenarios. This study introduces an innovative approach for analyzing time-correlated single photon counting data, where the rotational correlation function is optimised through a trajectory framework under constraints. By leveraging the constraints of normalized autocorrelation functions and values at zero and infinite time, the algorithm generates a distribution of possible functions. A notable benefit of this method is the ability to recover distorted experimental autocorrelation functions while accurately reconstructing the underlying distribution. We validate the technique's effectiveness by applying it to high-level molecular dynamics simulations and time-resolved experimental data of the beta-barrel protein cyanobacterium cyanobellin-1. The results demonstrate the method's capability to accurately extract the rotational correlation time from experimental data that has been distorted by resolution limitations. Furthermore, the study explores the relationship between the trajectory distribution and the overall dynamics, and we propose a metric to quantify the diversity of the trajectory distribution and assess the overall dynamics. The optimization of this metric, in conjunction with a cost matrix defined by the constraints, enables the generation of a distribution of possible evolutions for the molecular dynamics, even in the absence of experimental data. The method's potential for application to diverse fields is also discussed. The COVID-19 pandemic's widespread nature has led many countries to implement contact tracing as a crucial measure to contain the spread of the SARS-CoV-2 virus. Various mobile apps have been created to facilitate this process, which relies on location data and is critical for public health services, but raises significant concerns regarding user privacy. To address this issue, several recent approaches have been developed to safeguard user anonymity in contact tracing applications. This work compares the confidentiality capabilities of three prominent contact tracing systems – Exposure Notification, MoCa, and Nearby Places – which all utilize a single server architecture. To evaluate their security, we conducted a comprehensive analysis, creating a tool called Coronav\'irus-SUS that simulates a malicious server to analyze user location data. This tool was used to identify potential risks to users' privacy, such as pinpointing their daily activities and residential area, highlighting the importance of anonymity in contact tracing applications. While all analyzed systems leaked some user information, Exposure Notification provided the highest level of anonymity, followed closely by Nearby Places. In comparison, MoCa offered the lowest level of confidentiality. Our research also provided design guidelines to enhance the confidentiality of contact tracing systems, which can serve as a foundation for developing future, more secure systems. To the best of our knowledge, this work offers an innovative approach to evaluating the confidentiality of contact tracing systems, as well as exposing the limitations of previous exposure notification systems which failed to provide any confidentiality guarantees. Moreover, this extended version includes the registration numbers of the following studies: ESPT-2021-R-001, ESPT-2021-R-002, and ESPT-2021-R-003. Auxiliary frequency regulation is a key capability for these distributed systems to manage voltage fluctuations directly, without needing support from larger power plants. This capability is particularly important for energy storage systems to maintain stable voltage levels within the grid, even under varying load conditions. This study examines the role of auxiliary frequency in stabilizing power grid voltage and compares the voltage stabilization effectiveness of two energy storage systems, a vanadate battery and a red-flow vanadium red flow battery, to demonstrate their capabilities in supporting grid frequency and maintaining stable voltage levels. Experimental testing was conducted to validate the results, which showed that auxiliary frequency performance can be stabilized across a range of discharge rates, highlighting the importance of this capability for energy storage systems to operate efficiently within the grid, and the need for comprehensive analysis to evaluate an storage system's voltage stabilization capabilities before it can be deployed. This research has significant implications for operators of distributed energy storage systems to understand their role in supporting grid frequency and maintaining stable voltage levels, and to inform policy decisions for integrating and deploying these systems to support the grid. In the study of the Sun's internal rotation, travel-time in helioseismology plays a crucial role in determining the rotation rate of the core. However, the method's limitation in accurately measuring the core's rotation is the need to subtract the contribution of surface movements. This is because the technique interprets surface movements as an indirect indication of the core's movement due to the principle of light travel. This limitation has led to a significant issue of over-correction, resulting in an unrealistic constraint on the core's rotation rate. To mitigate this problem, this study assesses the impact of movements near active regions on travel-time measurements. By evaluating how these movements, such as those near active regions, near equators, and at the poles, affect the core's rotation rate, this study provides a solution to minimize their influence. This solution involves adjusting the side l=0 and l=1 components of the core's rotation profile. Applying the corrected methods to global seismograms, this study recalculates the core's rotation rate and finds that the rotation rate at the core's center can range between 450 to 680 nHz per second. This study's recalculated rotation rate lies within the range of prograde and antipode rotation rates derived from helioseismology and those observed on the surface. Furthermore, this study's results indicate that the rotation rate in the core's periphery can be as low as 100 nHz per second and demonstrates that the movement near active regions significantly contributes to the core's rotation rate measurement more so than other types of movements. Consequently, to accurately measure the core's rotation rate, researchers must consider the influence of movements near active regions and implement specific corrections in the l=0 and l=1 components. Applying these corrections results in a more realistic rotation rate in the core and helps minimize over-correction. This study provides essential insights for accurately determining the core's rotation rate in helioseismology and solar-dense matter helioseismology. The study's findings also shed light on the significance of movements near active regions in the core's rotation rate measurement and provides a potential explanation for the 55-day periodicity observed in the core's rotation rate, and this phenomenon can be attributed to the movement near active regions and the established 55-day activity cycle. In the near future, the proliferation of high-quality display technologies and advancements in light field capture and rendering will significantly rely on efficient light field image compression methods. A major challenge in compressing light field images is the significant increase in data size as the number of views increases. Our solution involves developing a novel, efficient compression technique that utilizes knowledge-based approaches to manage this challenge. Our solution model, 'Disparity,' which is also known as the Disparity-Conscious Model, incorporates a variational auto-encoder with multiple resolutions and an encoder-decoder architecture utilizing adaptive transform and progressive loss functions. These features enable our model to effectively compress light field images at high resolution, while the Disparity concept ensures spatial and temporal coherence in the images. During the evaluation process, our model performed competitively, while thorough analysis confirmed its ability to effectively compress light field images at high resolution, and its ability to represent images with varying disparities. Additionally, our model was found to leverage disparity information to create high-quality compressed images using relatively low number of views. For instance, it was able to generate high-quality compressed images from 16 views with significantly lower bitrates compared to the need for 60 views in the baseline approach. Using our model, it is possible to store a 60-view light field image at 24bpp in RGB space in two channels using 6 bits each, while the baseline approach compresses the image to 24.78bpp in RGB space in 16 channels using 0.4 bits each. Our research focuses on enhancing vector-based cross-lingual information retrieval by developing a dual framework comprising of both interactive and non-interactive models. In the non-interactive model, which we call the CLIR-DualEncoder, we employ an unsupervised cross-lingual retrieval framework that maps English and non-English documents into a single multilingual space using dual transformers. This framework combines query and document representations from both languages to compute a relevance score. We also explore and compare different joint training objectives for our model and find that a novel multilingual contrastive learning objective, which contrasts English and non-English representations with randomly selected pairs, yields the best results. On the other hand, our interactive model, which we call the CLIR-DualFramework, relies on pre-trained transformers that map English and non-English queries to a shared space. It uses a query translation module to translate queries from one language to another and computes a similarity score in the shared space. In the fine-tuning process, it leverages user feedback to adapt both the query translation and ranking components. We integrated our models into a variety of information retrieval systems, which we evaluated using multiple superscript datasets. The results show that our non-interactive model achieves a median performance equal to or better than that of NeuroIR-R. The CLIR-DualFramework achieved a median performance equal to or better than that of the best baseline in the Medline dataset. Furthermore, we observed significant gains in terms of high recall and 8-meter metrics when using both the CLIR-DualEncoder and CLIR-DualFramework in the Medline dataset. The former produced a 13% improvement in the 64-meter metric, while the latter produced a 12% improvement in the 8-meter metric. In this expanded model, the outcome is a positive or zero value, and the ratio of risk to reward is called the fractional stake. We analyze two scenarios: when the stake fraction and the payoff are described by continuous variables, and when they're part of a Gaussian distribution. When the stake and the payoff are normally distributed, we create a Hamiltonian and calculate the associated Schrödinger equation to find the optimal betting strategy. We also find a way to represent the conditional probability of a bet's success given its value. We introduce a new variable that, when squared, indicates the effectiveness of a bet, and we find its optimal value in both the continuous and Gaussian scenarios. We conclude by discussing how our findings can be applied, and how they can serve as a starting point for further research into more complex betting models. We also calculate the lifespan of a bank that starts with an initial amount of wealth. Our results show that, as the number of bets or the size of the time steps increases, the exponential growth of the bank's wealth still outpaces that of traditional betting strategies under similar conditions. Time series forecasting faces significant challenges in economics and business studies. One major issue is the difficulty in determining an optimal number of future time points for making predictions. Various models, including exponential smoothing, have been developed to tackle this problem, often relying on a parsimony principle to balance accuracy and complexity. This study introduces a novel approach by harnessing the strengths of hierarchical Bayesian models and variational inference to forecast multiple time steps simultaneously. Our model, called HBSm, leverages a hierarchical Dirichlet process prior to select the optimal number of future time points automatically. Additionally, we utilize a neural network-based regression model in a difference space to capture non-linear, continuous-time relationships between consecutive steps. Our results indicate that HBSm consistently selects a reasonable number of forecasting steps and performs well in predicting multiple future steps, often surpassing the performance of traditional exponential smoothing methods and outperforming a state-of-the-art dynamic linear model with variational inference on single-step forecasts. However, when piling up one-step predictions does not yield consistent performance in multi-step forecasting. Therefore, using a higher number of steps in piling up predictions, as in our approach, does not guarantee better multi-step forecasting performance. We present VLA and ALMA observations of Rho Ophiuchus, focusing on its brightest source, S1, a young stellar object within the cloud. We analyzed radio continuum, H30α, and CO and [CII] line emissions to understand the relationship between S1's outflow and the surrounding cloud's thermal gas. Analysis of radio continuum and H30α emissions indicate ionized gas sizes about 1.1 to 1.3 parsecs in diameter, while CO and [CII] line emissions suggest diameters of about 2 parsecs. By examining column densities and temperatures, we found that the [CII] emission in Rho Ophiuchus arises from atomic gas, primarily influenced by PDRs. This atomic gas has a column density around 3e21 cm^-2 and a temperature of about 35 K. Further, we discovered that the PDRs are primarily affected by the cloud's visual extinction, with a calibration offset of about 0.7 dex. By utilizing the C/O ratio, we found that the CO emissions could be the result of an internal jet, distinct from the wider, CO-emitting outflow. This outflow likely interacts with the cloud at velocities of about 20 km s^-1. By examining the interaction between S1's jet and the cloud, we found evidence of shock effects on the cloud's gas, primarily based on the widespread, hot gas within the cloud. This hot gas appears to be primarily stationary. By analyzing the momentum of S1's jet, we found it to be around 1.6e32 M sun per year^2, indicating the jet is momentum-driven. The Transformer model, first introduced in 2017, has rapidly become the premier choice for NLP tasks, surpassing traditional neural network models despite being inherently more complex. This review assesses the latest advancements in Transformer-based models for NLP, focusing on understanding the underlying mechanisms that set them apart from other models. We will examine the statistical properties of attention that inform the incorporation of informative features and the relevance of the input. We will also explore the effect of multitasking, model size, and data on the superiority of Transformer models, as well as the implications of their high complexity. Furthermore, this review delves into recent innovations in leveraging structural information in preprocessing, using character-level features, employing label smoothing, and using loss functions to improve model performance. We will review notable breakthroughs of state-of-the-art Transformer models in NLP and provide relevant code and model resources for the community. Finally, future challenges and opportunities for further research are identified. The related code and models can be found at https://github.com/satyag/Transformer-review.

Convolutional neural networks harness the convolutional operation's ability to exploit spatial relationships in data, making them inherently module-interpretable. We offer a novel perspective on why convolutional networks often perform better than similarly structured fully connected ones, specifically in image recognition tasks. Our analysis suggests that the key lies in the limited parameter redundancy present in convolutional networks, allowing each module to only represent its local neighborhood in data patterns. We visually illustrate and mathematically quantify the distinct regional focus captured by individual modules within a convolutional network compared to its fully connected counterpart, utilizing the MNIST dataset. Additionally, we provide empirical evidence from various image recognition tasks that the convolutional network's performance benefits directly from the reduced redundancy in its parameter space. Finally, we introduce an innovative trimming algorithm aimed at enhancing the performance of fully connected neural networks by eliminating parameter redundancy, thereby making them module-interpretable like their convolutional counterparts. Our study offers new insights into the mechanisms governing neural networks, particularly those employing full linking, and provides a practical solution to improve such networks. The proposed trimming algorithm can be applied not only to fully connected networks derived from convolutional ones but also to any type of neural network. Furthermore, we contend that the proposed algorithm's outcomes can serve as a benchmark to assess the performance of future algorithms designed to improve neural network parameters. Our study's code is available for use at https://github.com/mandar25/FCTRIM. Using the Indian Institute of Technology Delhi's NeHuR dataset https://sites.google.com/view/nikhiljha-research/datasets, we have empirically demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm on datasets containing natural images. One of the key outcomes of our study is that the proposed algorithm's effects are such that the performance of the network whose weights were trimmed by half is comparable to that of a larger network whose weights were trimmed by a quarter in the case of the dataset in question. We trust that the current research will stimulate the development of future work on neural network trimming and relevance-based weight trimming. The hybrid digital-analog approach, an innovative protocol that combines digital and analog elements in conjunction, represents a significant step towards bridging this implementation gap. The strategy involves generating the unitary evolution of a given quantum algorithm through digital control while utilizing an analog channel to produce the necessary states. The SF(v$_2$) symmetry flow of particles, such as electrons, muons, and hadrons, originating from beauty hadrons, was measured in central and ultracentral Pb-Pb collisions at a 5.02 TeV collision energy. These results were derived from ALICE at the LHC using track combinations from the ALICE Tracking System and the Electromagnetic Calorimeter. Compared to particles not coming from beauty hadrons, the calculated value of SF(v$_2$) indicates a significant elliptical deformation in particles from beauty hadrons, particularly in particles with lower transverse momentum, but shows lower than expected deformation for particles with higher transverse momentum. These results were compared to theoretical models, such as iTB and SMING, which successfully explain the data, suggesting that particles from beauty hadrons follow the general elliptic flow pattern. These findings reveal that particles coming from beauty hadrons follow the same collective flow behavior as other particles, but more theoretical validation is needed to fully understand this interaction. Additionally, the validation of these results will provide crucial insights into how individual heavy quarks interact and incorporate collective flow characteristics during hadronization. a novel approach to merging expert opinions is developed, utilizing the information
framework of Dempster-Shfer theory in conjunction with an innovative opinion
merging algorithm. An adaptable decision support system is introduced, capable of
handling unforeseen situations and scenarios. Experimental evaluation, conducted
using real-world human resource data, demonstrates the effectiveness and relevance
of the proposed solution in supporting organizational auditing with feature and class
adaptation. Furthermore, a comparative analysis highlights the benefits of combining
formal concept analysis and opinion mining, revealing how individual decision makers
are influenced by the data, and how combining their views leads to increased model
accuracy and relevance compared to using either method in isolation. Finally, the
research highlights potential avenues for further development and improvement.

The Strauss point process is a model that considers interactions between pairs of points within a bounded area. When no such interactions occur, the resulting spatial arrangement of points adheres to the complete spatial likelihood condition. Fuchs and Shapiro previously proposed an algorithm to generate points that conform to a complete spatial likelihood condition for a specific type of processes called multi-Hawkes processes. We have adapted their method, known as the CS method, and applied it to the Strauss process. Our approach involves dividing the area into non-overlapping squares and assigning Poisson intensities to each. We have developed two variants of this method, labelled Stitch and Refine. The Refine method is an enhanced version of the Stitch method, where points are refined within a smaller area. We have compared these methods to traditional algorithms such as the next arrival method and reverse time, and found that the Refine method yields more accurate results. Our average computation time for the Refine method is approximately 4.6 seconds for simulating 10000 points on a square with an area of 1, using two cores. We have also provided R code for these methods. We have found that the Refine method performs well even when simulating processes with intense interactions and high intensities. We suggest using the Refine method for simulating point processes, and acknowledge that this method can be extended to simulate multi-Hawkes processes. However, proposals generated by region-based and top-down object detection methods can be costly, involving the processing of numerous suboptimal suggestions. This tendency to produce excessive proposals, common in widely used object detection methods like Faster R-CNN, can result in proposal pool dilution due to the inclusion of less desirable candidates, negatively impacting the performance of pairwise models that rely on high-quality proposals to generate accurate predictions. This paper presents an innovative approach, Stable Pairing, an end-to-end method addressing proposal quality by incorporating a new mechanism that selectively makes proposals based on both objectness and spatial coherence. The proposed method demonstrates a significant enhancement in performance, achieving an average gain of 2% mAP over Faster R-CNN using IoU, an average improvement of 1% mAP when using other metrics, on the MS COCO dataset. Furthermore, experiments conducted on the Visual Genome dataset reveal a reduction in the number of proposals of 30% or more while maintaining high precision, indicating a substantial reduction in the dilution of proposal quality. The proposed method has also outperformed state-of-the-art object detection methods, achieving an average gain of 1% mAP over Cascade R-CNN and Faster R-CNN, and an average improvement of 0.5% mAP over R-FCN, on the MS COCO dataset. We develop a new group-wise sparse recovery method for noise-contaminated signals, which are measured using quadratic relationships. Our approach is inspired by recent advancements in Bilinear Compressive Sensing (BCS) techniques. By assuming a specific "bilinear mask" structure, we can achieve highly efficient and reliable signal recovery. Our theoretical bounds demonstrate superior recovery guarantees compared to the BCS method under similar quadratic measurements. Moreover, we outline a practical algorithm for BCS-based signal recovery and verify its effectiveness through various real-world data examples. Our results indicate that this algorithm can consistently produce high-quality signal estimates with minimal noise residuals, even in complex quadratic measurement scenarios. We also present a new quadratic measurement tool called the "Rapid Expanded Basis Positioning" (REBP) method, which incorporates features like global support detection, efficient signal restoration, and accurate location estimation. Our comparative analysis highlights the superiority of signal recovery achieved through the REBP method over other established techniques like Cramer-Rao and 2D Fourier Transform. By integrating our algorithmic design principles, we can develop reliable signal recovery methods for a broad range of quadratic observation models characterized by sparse or approximable signals, bilinear observation structures, and complex noise patterns. Our research focuses on the fundamental problem of signal recovery from quadratic observations, which is crucial for various applications. Our proposed algorithmic framework and theoretical analysis provide a comprehensive solution to this problem, encompassing various noise models and signal characteristics. We have also developed a general utility function for signal recovery, which can be extended to incorporate additional problem-specific constraints and noise models. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach, which outperforms existing techniques in terms of accurate signal recovery. Our algorithmic design principles and theoretical analysis provide a deeper understanding of the underlying problem, which is essential for addressing the challenge of signal recovery from quadratic observations. In response, we introduce BEVFusion - a simple yet powerful framework that fuses these two modalities through beam fusion, ultimately enhancing performance across beacon detection, point cloud fusion, and center line prediction tasks. To showcase its efficacy, we integrated this framework within the BeVFusion-RCNN architecture. The resulting model achieved exceptional results on the KITTI dataset, outperforming previous benchmarks. Notably, we obtained 78.6% and 82.2% increases in IoU metrics for LiDAR-only and image-only evaluations respectively, while maintaining a stable overall evaluation metric. Furthermore, our research highlights the importance of properly combining LiDAR and camera feeds, especially when utilizing distinct beam spacings. High-speed data processing technologies enable organizations to process massive amounts of information quickly, yet they often struggle with providing detailed and interactive insights to users, mainly due to limitations in storing and managing complete data sets. By applying this approach, analysts can produce informative and compact signatures that capture significant patterns and information in the data, allowing it to be stored and analyzed at high speeds. Our proposed system incorporates a visual framework and algorithms that utilize this signature to facilitate discovery and analysis of hidden patterns in the data, while also streamlining the processing of incoming data streams by identifying and extracting new instances of the detected patterns, and accurately estimating the data distribution based on the learned signature, further enhancing analysis and storage efficiency. Our evaluation shows the effectiveness of this approach in providing comprehensive insights and saving analysis and storage resources, as demonstrated by our experiments conducted on diverse business applications, such as marketing trends and disease surveillance. Our results indicate that the proposed signatures and analysis tools can be widely applicable across different domains and significantly enhance data analysis capabilities while streamlining processing and storage requirements. In a distinctive approach, a method called RENATO has been created, utilizing a set of rules based on cut diagrams to compute specific one-loop integrals accurately. A key benefit of RENATO lies in its ability to seamlessly integrate with leading-order amplitudes, thereby simplifying the calculation of meaningful observables. Specifically, applications of RENATO have yielded successful results for top and bottom quark production, both separately and combined in association. In a notable breakthrough, RENATO has successfully accounted for all non-resonant graphs in top and bottom production at leading order, effectively eliminating the need for additional subtraction terms. Given its versatility, RENATO is well-positioned to be utilized in various benchmark scenarios and theoretical models in the future. Furthermore, RENATO is being adapted to handle two-loop associators for semi-inclusive top and bottom production. In this updated version, RENATO will address the need for correction terms to address finite-width effects. The full benchmark suite is currently undergoing validation against existing results and will soon be released as a public code extension. Additionally, RENATO is being integrated with other frameworks such as SCET and SoftAct, with plans to expand its capabilities to various other processes in QCD. By combining RENATO with fixed-order cross sections, it has successfully produced reliable results for NLO and NNLO NLO and single differential rates for top and bottom production at the HL-LHC, using the SM input parameters from the 't Hooft 'unitary' system. Recently, RENATO has also been applied in a new version to correctly handle scale dependence in two-loop associators for top and bottom production, effectively demonstrating the reliability of RENATO in treating finite-width effects. The new version of RENATO, with enhanced capabilities for scale dependence, is poised to further expand its usability and applicability in the future. The full set of results from these applications of RENATO will be released as a public code extension called 'RENATO 2.0'. Currently, RENATO 2.0 is being further validated and refined to be fully compatible with the interface to the 't Hooft 'unitary' system for scale dependence. Following this update, it will be released as part of a new suite called 'PreciseNLO'. In recent years, SPARQL machine translation has received growing attention, yet it remains a challenging task due to SPARQL queries' inherent complexity. Traditional data enhancement methods that rely on approximate matching to retrieve similar data points are often unsuitable for SPARQL query datasets, leading to poor data quality and poor translation results. We introduce an innovative duplicate mechanism leveraging the inherent structure of SPARQL queries to address this issue. By integrating our new mechanism with a conventional data enhancement method, we observe improved query consistency and overall performance. Experimental validation through both manual and automated assessment confirms the effectiveness of our approach, demonstrating superior results compared to a baseline method in a SPARQL machine translation task. We have made our project's source code freely available.

This metric measures the impact and productivity of scholars by citing their work up to a specific age in time. Productivity is compared to a set of predetermined standards. By modifying Hirsch's original formula to calculate the h-(10)-index, which uses a more realistic set of standards, this study shows a significant reduction in the discrepancy between expected and actual productivity at the age of 40. Furthermore, this study introduces a new index that evaluates scholars based on particular venues and their performance at specific ages. By analyzing scholars who published at least one relevant paper at the age of 40, our study reveals that there's less difference between expected and actual performance post that age. By incorporating self-citation policies into the calculation of the v-h-(40)-index and the v-h-(10)-index, our study confirms that these indices adhere to the laws of cumulative distribution functions. With these indices, our study shows that venues significantly affect a scholar's productivity and this factor should be taken into consideration during research evaluation. By allowing the selection of relevant venues, our study reveals that researchers can customize their evaluation more effectively. We have conducted direct numerical simulations of rotating turbulent flows in a square box to investigate the spectral evolution of inertial waves. Contrary to the prevailing theory, our results indicate that wave energy adheres to the Kolmogorov spectrum $E(f) \sim f^{-7/3}$. Additionally, our data show wave anisotropy, linearly increasing with the Taylor number and relative to other energy components. Further analysis on wave straining and transport is underway to gain insight into the underlying mechanisms. Notably, these findings align with recent DNS and DNS-like numerical experiments by [Babin et al., 2016]. However, it is essential to consider additional factors in the far-inertial-range behavior, such as shell interactions mediated by forward enstrophy transfer, to enhance our understanding. Assuming these factors are negligible, we can infer that high-order Taylor series expansions of energy spectra may provide significant numerical insights. In the light of these observations, we suggest conducting multi-domain, high-resolution, large-domain DNS to explore deep into the inertial range. Such an approach may uncover critical numerical influences on spectral slopes and enable us to explore the convergence of spectra towards universal forms like $E(f) \sim f^{-1}$ in the very far-inertial-range. As for the $E(f)$ intercept, our results do not provide conclusive numerical evidence for or against the theory that it equals $\bar{\omega}^2/2$ in the idealized case or any numerical value in the finite-domain scenario. Lastly, we intend to integrate these insights into a comprehensive closure theory, which can be applied to diverse domains, including Earth's and other gaseous planets' inner ones. This study focuses on the thermodynamic properties of monolayer graphene electronically modulated by an external bias, which produces electrically induced bandgap opening. We employed the density functional theory using the local density approximation for our calculations and investigated the dependence of chemical potential, heat capacity, and entropy on temperature for different electrically induced bandgaps. Notably, our calculations showed that chemical potential within the bandgap exhibits non-linear temperature behavior, while heat capacity and entropy show two distinct patterns across the bandgap. We observed that the bandgap's temperature dependence follows a logarithmic pattern, increasing in a predictable manner with bandgap height. Our analysis revealed that electrically induced bandgaps within the range of 0.1 eV exhibit the largest contribution to entropy. Additionally, we compared our results with those of semiconducting and metallic materials, noting that electrically induced bandgaps of 0.1 eV can stimulate the same level of entropy as semiconducting materials and significantly higher than metallic materials. Finally, our calculations demonstrated that electrically induced bandgaps of 0.3 eV can stimulate the same level of entropy as semiconducting materials and significantly higher than metallic materials and bandgaps of 0.1 eV. Our work provides essential insights into the thermodynamic behavior of electronically modulated graphene, which can be applied in various electronic and photonic devices, as well as thermoelectric materials. We anticipate that our research will contribute to the development of innovative solid-state materials and devices. We encourage readers to further explore the underlying quantum mechanics of electronically induced bandgaps in graphene. The present findings can also inspire researchers working with superconductors, semiconductors, and metallic materials to modulate their bandgap and thermodynamic properties manually. For example, electronically inducing a 0.3 eV bandgap in metallic materials like copper results in the formation of semiconductor-like materials, characterized by chemical and electrical conductivity similar to those of semiconducting materials. Furthermore, researchers can manually convert superconductors into semiconductor materials by introducing a 0.3 eV bandgap, preserving their electrical conductivity while converting their chemical conductivity. These breakthroughs offer unprecedented opportunities for the development of innovative solid-state materials and devices. Recent findings have established that low-energy radiation from active binary star CR Draconis is likely generated by a magnetized plasma in its corona, triggered by flares. Observations from 2016 and 2017, conducted simultaneously by optical telescopes and radio frequency receivers at various frequencies, identified eight radio frequency events with a frequency range of approximately 0.5 to 16 GHz. High-resolution images of flares at optical frequencies often show chromatic activity, a broader pattern that the observed radio frequency data using the UDA radio telescope may be replicating. Our innovative neural rendering technique transforms a virtual human avatar's 3D mesh into a neural network, enabling support for highly customizable, non-rigged characters in applications like virtual try-on, game animation, and interactive environments. As these characters are often designed to be highly articulated, we've developed an advanced visualization tool to help artists understand and visualize the following rendering processes: (1) how the neural network generates images from 3D poses, (2) which neural network components influence image generation, and (3) how the output images are composed. This visualization tool facilitates detection of potential rendering issues, enables artists to identify areas where models fall short, and reveals unexpected visual effects. Moreover, we've created a user-friendly interface for adjusting character parameters, such as pose, camera view, illumination, and attachments like clothing and accessories. Our ANR tool enhances collaboration and communication among artists, making it clear how certain features appear and how artifacts are caused by specific configurations, such as attachments or camera angles. We used our technique to create novel effects in our demo video by modifying parameters like clothing, hand poses, and camera angles. Our approach also outperforms existing methods in terms of memory efficiency, running efficiently at a frame rate of nearly 30 FPS on a high-end GPU. An interactive demonstration of our technique can be accessed at a website controlled by a neural network. The source code for our method has been made available for public use. Probing redshift z > 6 through spectroscopic means poses a significant challenge, and as a result, large far-infrared to submillimeter survey programs face difficulties in obtaining high-confidence redshifts above z = 6. Fortunately, strong rotational lines in molecular gases provide reliable and distinctive absorption features that can be used to accurately determine very high redshifts. Although the number of detected features in this range is limited, a theoretical model has been developed to predict the occurrence of these features at specific redshifts. So far, one strong H2 absorption feature has been detected at z = 2.034, as well as three lines at z = 4, z = 5, and z = 7 in line of sight towards the galaxy HLTON 1. These discoveries, combined with an analysis of radio interstellar medium (ISM) observations, have led to the identification of two ISM redshift candidates at z = 6 and z = 7. However, unambiguous redshifts have not been obtained as they are based on radio data alone. A comprehensive analysis of far-infrared to submillimeter data using the ALMA, NOEMA, and SPICA telescopes is necessary to further investigate the occurrence of H2, H3+, and CO absorption as well as emission in strong-field objects across the entire far-infrared to submillimeter spectrum. A proposed experiment aims to detect these features and determine the redshifts of the strongest features in a small field of view using SPICA, a 60-4000 μm passive infrared space telescope. By employing an innovative approach where the position of the telescope's beam is treated as an element of a Sudoku puzzle, the instrument can identify objects with stable redshifts. A change in the beam's position will result in a shift in the observed redshift, and by observing the same object multiple times at different beam positions, the instrument can accurately determine the redshift. A simulation of this experiment reveals that two of these SPICA experiments can provide unambiguous evidence for the presence of H2 in HLTON 1 at z = 7 with a redshift of 6.06 and 6.70. A third experiment, however, has failed to produce a redshift for H3+ in the galaxy G035. Foster at z = 4.434. These predicted redshifts serve as essential benchmarks for future far-infrared to submillimeter survey programs, and their occurrence is crucial in addressing certain fundamental cosmological questions. Our research delves into the possibilities of utilizing large pre-trained language models as semantic analyzers, enabling them to accurately interpret novel expressions whose meanings were gleaned from existing ones. To achieve this, we develop a method of fine-tuning these models with just a few key examples from each new context, relying on pre-existing models' inherent semantic understanding. The results indicate that even minimal training yields notable improvements in processing unfamiliar terms as part of familiar sentences, particularly showing that models can learn to effectively generalize from short instructional sequences containing contextual pointers, like hyperlinks. The developed technique enables sophisticated applications like constructing custom lexicons, toolkits for generating text based on evidence, and algorithms to simulate conversations, all requiring no additional user input beyond providing relevant examples, eliminating the need for direct supervision during model fine-tuning. The research highlights the potential for substantial enhancements by leveraging large pre-trained language models as semantic analyzers. HD58260, a 0.5d B-type star, exhibits significant magnetic field variability, with field strengths ranging from 610 to 2150 Gauss. OMI$\phi$-polarimetry revealed an extraordinary magnetic field output on March 11, 2019, characterized by a rapid field fluctuation from a field strength of 1140 Gauss in the first collected spectrum to 2150 Gauss in the last, collected over a time frame of approximately 20 minutes. This rapid field shift surpasses the time it takes magnetic energy to transfer throughout the entire star, indicating that external factors must be influencing the magnetic field on such short timescales. Temporal knowledge graphs have recently gained attention due to their ability to effectively encode dynamic and time-sensitive information into graph-like structures using temporal annotations. An essential task for maintaining the accuracy and completeness of these graphs is predicting future links. Existing link prediction methods typically rely on training models from comprehensive knowledge graph datasets on an ongoing basis using new data as it becomes available, a strategy requiring continuous retraining and frequent updates when the graph undergoes significant changes. Building upon the concept of static graph frameworks, our approach leverages a single static model to predict links across the entire graph, regardless of the arrival time of new data. By utilizing a unified representation of past and future time periods, our method effectively handles data from various time intervals. Thoroughly tested on real-world datasets, the results confirm that our approach outperforms existing link prediction techniques. Additional analysis highlights the importance of incorporating a time-aware mechanism to refine predicted score calculations and also reveals that our approach effectively handles diverse knowledge graph domains. An implementation of our method is now publicly available to facilitate further research. Evaluation results and our code can be found at the provided repository address. The pursuit of high-energy femtosecond pulses in Kerr-lens frequency-doubling soliton lasers necessitates a thorough understanding of their operation. Contrary to popular belief, the sole determinant of soliton formation is not simply the net group-delay dispersion but requires consideration of the cavity's complex frequency-dependent group-delay dispersion and soliton self-frequency shift. We present a detailed analysis of soliton formation in actively resonant cavities, examining the behavior of solitons as they circulate within the cavity and providing the criteria for soliton frequency-doubling without nonlinear phase modulation. This theoretical work is further validated by an experimental verification. This fundamental analysis is expected to be particularly significant in solid-state lasers that generate high-peak-power pulses measuring micrometers due to their extended gain spectra. Finally, we explore the potential limitations of soliton formation in future high-energy soliton lasers. Soliton frequency-doubling holds great promise for generating tunable few-hundred millijoule pulses in the near-infrared range, enabling the creation of ultrashort pulses with energies of up to 100 attoseconds. We discuss the potential applications of soliton frequency-doubling in future high-energy soliton lasers. Although SFA shifts the soliton's frequency into the mid-infrared range, we present a novel approach for tuning soliton frequency to the 2.3-2.4 micron range via dispersion-controlled frequency-doubling, offering a versatile method for generating tunable pulses in the near-infrared range. This frequency-tuning method is anticipated to be particularly significant in future high-energy soliton frequency-compression lasers. Early detection of depression is crucial for effective treatment and rehabilitation.  While standard clinical assessment tools are reliable, they have one major drawback: they only offer a snapshot of mental health at a particular moment, which may not necessarily predict future behavior or activity.  In contrast, social media can provide more nuanced insights into an individual's well-being, making it a valuable resource for identifying mental health issues, including depression.  Previous studies have attempted to develop methods for automatically detecting depression from social media content, but they have been hindered by limited data sets and the lack of thorough evaluations.  To address these limitations, we have compiled a substantial dataset of annotated social media posts from patients who have been diagnosed with depression or bipolar disorder, as well as non-depression controls.  Our dataset is distinctive because it features posts written by individuals who have been clinically diagnosed with depression, creating a more accurate standard against which to compare control groups.  In order to illustrate the value of large datasets and thorough evaluations, we have conducted two studies that classify depression from social media content.  The first study involved identifying depression from a transcribed representation of social media content, while the second involved using visual content from social media posts.  By providing a detailed analysis of our results, as well as identifying potential areas of improvement, we hope to inspire the development of more advanced techniques for automatically detecting depression on social media. In a new approach to matrix compression, we explore matrices with entries drawn from various distributions within distinct subgroups. Focusing on rank-one matrix compression, we consider the impact of a finite number of these distributions and show that as the size of the matrix increases, the results of matrix compression converge to a weighted average of the corresponding limits for matrices with entries drawn from the individual distributions. The convergence is to a matrix composed of weighted sine series, where the coefficients of these series correspond to the weights. The ultimate application of this finding is the development of a new model for oil reserve prediction that combines sine series and S-shaped growth models. The proposed method outperforms existing compression techniques in this predictive task. The theoretical conclusions also provide a framework for the asymptotic analysis of matrix compression in this more complex setting. The effectiveness of the proposed method was demonstrated using real-world datasets, including a collection of matrices related to the analysis of rock formations from hydraulic fractures. The accompanying source code is available on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/tuomakangas/Matrix-Compression-with-Groupwise-Heterogeneity. The source code includes the implementation of matrix compression and the sine series in the Julia programming language, as well as the data used in our numerical experiments. The results presented here form the basis of a more extensive dissertation on this topic by the first author, which can also be accessed via the provided GitHub repository. Originally conceived as a payment system, the blockchain's potential has expanded into supporting decentralized applications, with its adoption accelerating across various sectors. Notably, the application of blockchain technology in marketplaces has gained momentum. We are examining the benefits and drawbacks of utilizing blockchain technology in marketplaces and exploring its capabilities to enable secure, trustworthy, and transparent online transactions. In various fields such as medicine, social sciences, and biology, researchers often analyze incomplete data, prompting the adoption of sensitive statistical methods. When dealing with missing data, researchers face challenges in assessing its impact, a problem we address by developing a novel Bayesian approach. Our strategy involves marking uncertain data points as 'questionable' and assigning them a range of possible values following a predictive distribution. To gauge the influence of individual questionnaires on the model, we compare 'questioned' data points with their 'unquestioned' counterparts. Building on the concept of the influential measure 'E-value', we create a Bayesian analogue, 'E-q', to quantify the likelihood that replacing 'questioned' data with unqestioned values would alter parameters. Moreover, 'E-q' facilitates parameter estimation via a Monte Carlo method, allowing for the simulation of replaced data and corresponding inference results. Utilizing 'E-q', we can determine whether missing data is problematic at a chosen confidence level. Our approach was successfully demonstrated in the field of social sciences using Monte Carlo simulations and a real-world question answering case study. Ultimately, the method may be applied to a range of Bayesian statistical models, potentially expanding its use to various data analysis scenarios. The proposed method has been incorporated into an R package named bayesID. Additional information about the research is available on the website through the button 'Supplementary Material'. We examined a sample of 1 million Python projects to compare best practices with actual cryptographic implementations, and found that 76% of projects use cryptographic primitives incorrectly, despite 35% of code being correct in terms of syntax, indicating a problem with logic or semantics. These incorrect implementations pose significant risks, potentially allowing attackers to bypass $70$ million in annual payments via Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard protocols due to a missing requirement. We discovered that a significant portion of Python projects receive little or no maintenance, and have not been updated or executed since their initial creation, which means they may not be subject to regular security audits, but could still pose security risks if exploited by attackers. Furthermore, we found that a substantial number of Python projects rely on third-party libraries, which can introduce security vulnerabilities if those libraries are misused, as we observed happens 57% of the time. We identified specific security risks, such as unencrypted HTTPS data in 38% of code and potentially insecure FLOSS usage in 21% of code, and recommended several security improvements to protect against common attacks like REAMDE, SSL/TLS, WebShell, and POODL. In summary, our research reveals the extent of security vulnerabilities in cryptographic implementations across various Python projects, and suggests a need for better security practices, greater awareness about secure coding, and more effective maintenance in third-party libraries and code repositories. The development of scalable, detailed, and rich urban environments in virtual worlds has significant implications for various fields, including virtual and augmented reality, urban planning, and geographic information systems. To create and update extensive urban scenes efficiently, we developed a voting-based system that can digitize urban settings with minimal user involvement. This system relies on users providing geometric and image-based data, which is then annotated through a voting process. To enhance the annotation process, we incorporated multi-angle 2D images and 3D color-coded mesh data. We evaluated our approach by comparing different-scale voting processes and assessing its robustness to various levels of user involvement. Through a crowd-sourcing study involving over 1,000 participants, we demonstrated our approach to be reliable and efficient, with the potential to transform the fields of urban visualization and geographic information systems. Further research will focus on adapting this approach for individual city blocks and buildings. Additionally, the virtual assistant restructures the requirements into a more suitable format, simplifying the specification generation. This method is particularly effective due to its simple implementation and high error-correction efficiency. By using it in superconducting qubits, it's possible to significantly reduce the complexity associated with conventional error-correction algorithms, utilizing a classical computer. This method can also be applied to a wide range of quantum encodings, making it a versatile tool. The model is applied to analyze relationships between oceanic phenomena, including the synchronization of storms and sea level anomalies, and its validity is verified through simulations. Recently, vision-language pre-training has gained significant attention, and various models have been proposed to enhance its performance. A key component of modern vision-language models is Contrastive Language- Vision (CLIP), which relies on text-based guidance for optimizing pre-trained vision models. However, current CLIP models have limitations due to visual noise and missing information in text descriptions, which hinder effective contrastive learning. To address these challenges, a new approach is introduced, which combines text and visual data to refine pre-trained vision models and enhance vision-language representation quality. This proposed technique, known as VT-CLIP, leverages visual hints to smoothen text-based descriptions and remove noise, thereby improving the quality of vision-language representations. Through extensive testing on various tasks, such as image-captioning and few-shot learning, VT-CLIP achieves state-of-the-art results and significantly outperforms existing models, demonstrating a 2.5 times improvement in image MS-COCO retrieval accuracy and a 9% increase in FLICv2 composite score, along with a 10% boost in FLICv2 semantic score. Additionally, VT-CLIP exhibits superior performance on 1-shot, 2-shot, 5-shot, and 10-shot tests within the FLICv2 dataset, and it also surpasses other models in performance on the ABLI dataset. This work is further validated through comprehensive ablation studies and exploration of its potential applications and extensions. The project's code and datasets are available for further use and analysis at https://github.com/whwu/vt-clip.

In the fields of pathology and radiology, image analysis provides qualitative or quantitative outcomes accompanied by explanatory texts. Such explanations, typically entered manually, can take the form of free-text based on the observer's skills and experience. To rectify this issue, we developed highdicom, an open-source Python tool that facilitates standardized encoding of image remarks and model outputs in the DICOM format. This is made possible by integrating the deepdicom library, which allows for the seamless interaction between deep learning model outputs and digital image files. Highdicom also optimizes model outputs for direct use in other DICOM software, while generating results in a readable format with the addition of qualitative comments. To demonstrate its capabilities, we employed our tool for predicting breast cancer subtypes from histopathological images and lymph nodes from radiographs. The project's source code and a detailed user's guide are now publicly available for adoption in research and clinical settings. By promoting its utilization, we believe highdicom can contribute to the creation of a collaborative, multi-center workflow for computer-aided diagnosis and therapy. Additionally, we aim to contribute to the ongoing standardization efforts in this area. The tool can be freely accessed via GitHub at https://github.com/constantinhein/highdicom, with a corresponding demonstration video available online at https://youtu.be/apiC-6i3yNo. Additionally, a highdicom powered study on breast cancer cell classification in histopathological whole-slide images has been deposited in the CCDC database with the identifier 'HC-WS-BreastCaCells'. The human genome is comprised of DNA, arranged in a double helix structure, where base pairs repeat in a specific sequence. Our task involves analyzing short DNA segments to identify representations that can be used for classification purposes. Given the inherent complexity and variability of genomic data, we develop an unsupervised, unstructured approach to representation learning, where a flexible autoencoder model is trained on pre-existing, publicly available genomic data without initial labeling, before applying an unsupervised clustering method to its latent representation. We then utilize human-cell specific base pair patterns in a supervised clustering scheme following representation learning to assess the effectiveness of our method. Our experimental results across multiple configurations validate the quality of our representations and their potential utility in classification tasks, while highlighting areas for further improvement. These representations are intended for use in downstream classification tasks, such as identifying specific species of DNA. Our source code is available for review on GitHub at https://github.com/tomfsarns/unixar/. Additionally, our research findings suggest several promising avenues for further investigation. Firstly, we could adapt our model to accommodate varying sequence lengths. Given that shorter sequences, comprising fewer base pairs, are less susceptible to errors and easier to analyze, our approach is well-suited for application. We propose employing a combination of several learned representations, where each corresponds to a specific sequence length, in a manner that mimics the characteristics of the problem at hand. Our research also suggests that we could improve representation quality by incorporating an additional module that recognizes repeated patterns in the data. We propose employing a relatedness metric to identify correlations between various sequence lengths and incorporating this information into our model. Our research also involves the analysis of representation quality through synthetic data, where we propose employing a synthetic analysis technique to identify the most crucial factors contributing to the problem at hand. Finally, our research involves the analysis of representation quality through accuracy, achieved by incorporating the identified patterns into a simple classifier. By incorporating these suggestions, we believe that the quality of our representations can be further improved. These representations are intended for use in a variety of applications, such as identifying species of DNA, to name one such potential use. The way the surface is arranged fundamentally influences most physical processes occurring on surfaces. To gain insight into its impact on the electronic transitions within ultrathin films, we examined how the surface termination affects the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$(0001) films. By using scanning tunneling microscopy and photoemission spectroscopy on well-defined V$_2$O$_3$ films with different surface terminations, we discovered a correlation between the surface termination and the presence of excess electrons. These measurements revealed that a change in surface termination leads to a change in electronic behavior, which results in a metal-insulator transition. In contrast to previous studies, our work indicates that the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ films is not triggered by changes at corundum surfaces but are instead controlled by the presence of excess electrons at the surface, which are facilitated by the different terminations. These findings have significant implications for the use of V$_2$O$_3$ in advanced technologies due to its potential to support various electronic states. Furthermore, our work highlights the value of using different surface terminations to access distinct electronic configurations within systems that undergo metal-insulator transitions. Ultimately, our study demonstrates the importance of considering the impact of surface termination on the electronic properties of materials, which is crucial for advancing our understanding of electronic phenomena and developing innovative technologies. By using a simple electronic model, our work also sheds light on the role of surface termination in mediating the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ films through the interaction between surface termination-induced excess electrons and the V$_3d$-O$_4p$ bands. These findings provide new insights into the complexity of electronic behavior that can arise on surfaces, which is influenced by various factors including symmetry and mediating energy levels. By acknowledging the significance of surface termination in determining metal-insulator transitions and electronic configurations, our work may inspire the development of new materials with tailored electronic properties. The classical Clebsch formulation offers an alternative way of describing certain Hamiltonian systems by expressing them in terms of momentum densities and canonical $n$-form. When applied to Lie-Poisson systems, this alternative formulation must accommodate changes in momentum frame. A general strategy has been developed for making Lie-Poisson systems over $\mathfrakg^*$ Clebschizable. The procedure involves first applying a specific coordinate transformation based on the coadjoint orbit map. By doing so, the system's Hamiltonian or Casimir functions can be re-expressed in a gradient or constant-by-constants-of-the-Clebsch-variables form. By employing this redefinition of momentum along with the coadjoint orbit map, various Lie-Poisson systems over $\mathfrakg^*$ can be Clebschized. An illustration of this procedure is provided using the heavy top. Additionally, the newly developed methodology has been used to find new or alternative integrals for a few Lie-Poisson systems, as well as some results previously obtained using the inverse Kostant-Suris mapping. Moreover, the utility of symplectic leaf geometry within the Clebsch formulation has been highlighted in finding these new integrals. The text also discusses the dualization of the multi-Hamiltonian Clebschization procedure of the bi-Hamiltonian structure, which was first described by Tsiganov. By considering the dual of bi-Hamiltonianity, the authors derive the method of dual bi-Hamiltonian Clebschization. This method is then successfully applied to the Lie-Poisson system over the $\mathfrak{se}(2)^*$ manifold describing a particle moving on a plane with gyroscopic action. Using the newly developed methods, the authors show that this system possesses a new, planar Poisson structure, which, along with its Lie-Poisson system over $\mathfrak{se}(2)^*$, is also solvable. An illustration of the first integral is provided using the properties of symplectic leaf geometry. Moreover, the text demonstrates the application of the dualization procedure in finding the first-order Hamiltonian orthonormal frame of a Lie-Poisson system over the $\mathfrak{se}(3)^*$ manifold describing a rigid body moving in three-dimensional space with gyroscopic action. Using the newly developed methods, the authors show that the impact of gyroscopic action can be eliminated by expressing the momentum frame using gyroscopic momentum and angular velocity. Predicting the lifespan of products, especially those with deteriorating properties like batteries, is crucial for preventing accidents and ensuring industry efficiency. We compare several machine learning models using data from non-functional battery samples, including features extracted via acoustic emission and energy discharge. Our goal is to determine the most effective survival analysis model and the relative importance of individual features. We aim to contribute to a safer world by enabling industry to accurately predict battery lifespans, thus reducing the risk of accidents. This study compares the performances of seven algorithms: Random Forest, Artificial Neural Networks, Support Vector Machine, KNN, Gradient Boosting, Linear Model, and Gradient Boosting Expert. Feature selection and analysis, as well as model comparisons, are conducted based on metrics such as RMSE, MBE, accuracy, F1 score, and feature importance, calculated from cross-validation evaluations. Our findings reveal that the KNN algorithm exhibits the lowest RMSE among the compared models, while the Acoustic features show significantly more variance compared to Energy features. Feature importance results reveal that the Energy Acoustic features have the highest consistency among all features. This research highlights the advantages and disadvantages of each algorithm and suggests selecting KNN for future projects, recommending feature importance analysis across multiple features for comparison and subsampling within the Energy group for practical applications. This report lays the groundwork for discussing the most effective survival analysis models and the relative importance of features, while identifying areas for improvement and practical considerations. It also opens the door for future discussions on practical applications and potential avenues of inquiry. Early detection and prevention of COVID-19 are crucial for preventing the spread of the virus. Accurate identification of the disease is achieved through chest CT scans in patients who have recently traveled, come into contact with others, or exhibit symptoms. However, finding lung nodules in these scans can be difficult for doctors to do, especially when the images are taken at low doses and show fewer details. Therefore, there is a need for deep learning-based software systems that can alert doctors to potential cases by processing these scans. 

We developed CovidCT-2nd, a double-staged capsule network system, to improve the accuracy of detecting COVID-19 in these scans. Capsule networks were chosen for this task because they surpass the performance of other architectures, such as convolutional neural networks, in detecting patterns with robustness. However, the initial capsule module's ability to distinguish between classes is not as strong as others, so we had to improve it. 

We combined the capsule output with two additional modules: an original capsule module, and a segmentation module. The original capsule module helps to identify the lung area, while the capsule segmentation module identifies the lung area and helps to distinguish between patterns. 

We tested CovidCT-2nd on the CT scans of 3,172 patients who had COVID-19 and 3,972 patients who didn't. For low-dose CT scans, the accuracy of the system was higher than others, with an accuracy of 88.54% and a mean average precision of 85.42%. 

In comparison, the system's accuracy on standard-dose CT scans was higher, with an accuracy of 90.09% and a mean average precision of 87.99%. 

We also compared our system to several other methods, with results showing that it surpassed them in detecting patterns at low-dose CT scans.

This concept led to the development of STP, a C++ framework and Python interface built upon BLAS and LAPACK, which achieves precise one-pass computations for optimal transport in just linear time, accompanied by a nearly linear time approximation algorithm, all while ensuring accurate results by avoiding potential cancellations. STP's unique two-fold functionality includes not only computing optimal transport but also generating smoothed sign functions. Furthermore, STP's implementation includes various useful and cross-platform functions, such as sampling according to a smoothed sign function and approximating its derivative. Specifically in the context of optimal transport, our library provides: (i) a precise one-pass approximation algorithm, (ii) a linear time, linear memory, and logarithmic depth algorithm, (iii) a blockwise approximation algorithm with a block-based approach, and (iv) a random smoothing-based average cost algorithm. Additionally, our library incorporates advanced solutions for multi-marginal optimal transport problems. Our approach also extends to the dynamic optimal transport problem through a new method using collinear triangular matrices to solve for the conservation law $u_t = au - bu$. AU Mic, a young star surrounded by a vast disk and at least two planetary candidates, has been identified as a rare YSO model exhibiting "dormant" T Tauri behavior. We have obtained a unique observational record of this star, capturing both "dormant" and "active" states and tracking the evolution of its FUV continuum and X-ray emission over nearly 5 years. The data reveals that AU Mic's FUV emission closely follows the star's X-ray emission in both intensity and variability patterns. Furthermore, by analyzing the spectral energy distribution of its FUV emission, we have determined its contribution to the stellar and planetary radii and temperatures. However, the resulting estimates are likely to be distorted by the impact of AU Mic's X-ray and FUV emission, suggesting that AU Mic b and c are likely to be true giants rather than hot planets. If so, this would explain why AU Mic b shows little to no rotation, aligning instead with the prograde rotation of its parent star. With the aid of numerical modeling, we have investigated possible scenarios for the physical mechanisms driving the X-ray and FUV emission in AU Mic, with the result that its X-ray emission is most likely generated by AU Mic's corona, the same source responsible for producing its FUV emission through either the same physical process or the presence of two separate emission regions. AU Mic's observed FUV and X-ray variability could then be attributed to fluctuations in the emission of AU Mic's coronal region. The resulting light curve models have further enabled us to gain a more detailed understanding of the behavior and properties of AU Mic's coronal region and its relation to its disk and planetary system. Specifically, the observed and predicted light curve behavior supports the presence of two separate emission regions, with the FUV emission of AU Mic potentially originating either from the same coronal region responsible for its X-ray emission or from a fan-shaped emission region. By analyzing the UV radiation of AU Mic, researchers have found that its disk could be exposed to the harsh conditions of its stellar X-rays. As a result, the formation of AU Mic's planets and the habitability of its planetary system may be impacted by the behavior and properties of AU Mic's coronal region. Future space-based observations of AU Mic and other young stellar objects in similar categories could significantly advance our understanding of the behavior and properties of their stellar coronal regions and their implications for their planetary systems. One model represents the drag experienced by a substance in the presence of moving charged particles, which is later applied to account for the behavior of nucleons and electrons within a star. Our research shows that the resulting radiation drag-induced motion in stars can be explained by a damped oscillatory or exponential decay. We also simulate how this effect might impact the equatorial plane of stars, such as the Sun, causing slight periodic changes or depression in their inner layers. The possibility that this phenomenon could explain minor irregularities in the Sun's motion is discussed. In addition, our models are used to speculate on the Sun's evolution and the role of viscous or resistive media in this process. Finally, our research highlights the possibility that stars could develop into white dwarfs through exponential decay in their inner layers. Additionally, our white dwarf simulation shows that the star's motion could exhibit reverse rotation due to this phenomenon. We introduce a new task known as perpetual view generation. The goal is to create a generative model that produces views not seen during training. Existing generative models are ineffective at generating novel, unseen viewpoints. To address this challenge, we have developed a conditional diffusion model called DiffDreamer, trained on the NCM dataset with 4000 pairs of synthetic images. By utilizing image rotation data and latent code conditionality, DiffDreamer models the spatial mapping of a scene's appearance across different view angles. Through continuous learning, DiffDreamer generates realistic, semantically sound views with novel perspectives, surpassing traditional generative models in quality and novelty. Not only does it outperform previous models in generating novel, unseen viewpoints, but it also produces more realistic single-view inputs that have not been observed during training. To ensure model robustness, we have developed a simple, efficient, and accurate latent code estimator, to provide transparent insights into the model's reasoning. To support future research, we have publicly released our code and pre-trained models for the N15.5 dataset and the NCM dataset. The models and code can be found on our website https://sites.google.com/view/const-learn-view. Additionally, we have provided an interactive demo at https://diffdreamer.net. This study proposes a novel control framework rooted in data-oriented principles. It seamlessly integrates predictive models, allows for post-hoc analysis, and controls epidemic outbreaks. This alternative representation retains crucial geometric and epidemiological properties of networks. A method for constructing a weighted super-network is developed, which enables the analysis of multiple networks using a single set of parameters. By leveraging this super-network structure, an improved dynamic system is constructed, allowing for the prediction of epidemic outbreaks and controlling their progression. A data-driven method for determining separation distances in large networks is also presented. Finally, an exploration of future research directions is provided, laying the groundwork for applying data-driven approaches to processes beyond epidemiology.
