The dynamics of a liquid layer on a fiber are investigated through a model of viscous flow, which incorporates capillary and gravitational forces as well as forces related to fiber surface tension. When a certain condition is met, perturbations on the fiber surface grow, causing the liquid layer to break up into droplets of varying sizes, larger than the initial wavelength of the perturbations. This instability is heightened by lower viscosity or steeper slopes, and by increasing either surface tension or gravitational force, but not by fiber diameter, according to simulations and experiments. Observations from experiments align with theoretical predictions, and indicate that this instability is a relevant factor in the formation of non-uniform droplets during fiber spinning and spinning fibers. A correlation between theoretical and experimental outcomes is established through analysis of droplet sizes, which shows that three factors – viscosity, surface tension, and density – combine to determine droplet sizes through a relationship that is confirmed through data. Our work provides a basis for understanding how combinations of factors like surface and fiber tension influence droplet formation during fiber spinning processes. This understanding can be applied to a range of materials, such as spinning fibers and biological processes like Pollen transfer and seed dispersal. Enabling efficient sharing of feature maps in multi-input multi-output (MIMO) architectures is crucial for reducing parameter count, a challenge that has stumped researchers so far. They've explored different ways to promote feature sharing, but it seems the field is still in its early stages. To make progress, we're proposing a straightforward yet effective method for facilitating feature sharing in MIMO structures. We're initially examining the MIMO method's ability to share feature maps in depth-based models, such as ResNet. We're also extending this idea to other model types, like transformer networks, with promising results so far. Furthermore, we're exploring ways to make our approach compatible with pre-trained models, and it just so happens that it can be applied seamlessly to both MIMO and standard depth-based models with equivalent results, according to our tests. We're also running some additional experiments to validate our approach. Overall, our feature sharing method appears to be highly effective, bringing about improvements in both computational efficiency and model performance. To demonstrate this, we're testing various models with different numbers of feature maps, and it seems the more feature maps a model has, the more pronounced the benefits become. We're also running some experiments to see how our approach handles different sizes of MIMO methods, and it seems the more compact designs benefit more significantly. We're also testing various datasets to validate our approach, and it seems our method is highly effective on different types of data. All things considered, our simple yet effective feature sharing method appears to be highly beneficial in reducing parameters in MIMO structures while still yielding better results than standard depth-based models, at least in our tests. We hope that others will find this work helpful and that it will contribute to further advancements in MIMO structures. Dataset availability and data quality significantly influence the accuracy of tasks involving document image analysis. This survey evaluates historical record image datasets in terms of their composition and challenges. It provides an in-depth analysis of the problems associated with the data, a comprehensive list of available datasets, a comparative assessment of their characteristics, and an exploration of future directions to overcome the prevalent data limitations. The primary objectives of the survey are two-fold: first, it aims to make the dataset information more accessible to researchers and practitioners, and second, it seeks to raise awareness about the inherent challenges associated with document image analysis datasets. Moreover, its reliance on straightforward arithmetic operations prevents computational complexity issues. The effectiveness of this position correction technique was evaluated through experiments involving an FANUC R-2000A robot. The results show that using raw position data yields a average position error of approximately 4.6 mm. By employing our position correction technique, this error is reduced to around 0.76 mm. A comparison of the resulting paths, obtained using both corrected and uncorrectored position data, confirms that the position correction method is accurate, with measured average distances between points of approximately 0.76 mm. A subsequent analysis, using the root-mean-square averaged norm, of the resulting velocity profiles, reveals a slight slowdown, with a decrease of around 3%, resulting from the position correction. Furthermore, experiments involving sinusoidal and random motion demonstrate a maximum detected bias of approximately 8 mm. The position correction technique is found to be effective up to a certain threshold speed, beyond which increased position errors are observed. Following a detailed noise analysis, we discovered that incorporating the position information into the robot's control loop eliminates path deviations. Consequently, our approach enhances both the position tracking accuracy and path stability of industrial robots equipped with auxiliary sensors providing detailed motion data. By exploiting this estimate, we derive a dimension-dependent bound for the norm of the interpolation operator, which can be explicitly stated for dimensions d ≥ 3. Furthermore, we examine scenarios where the given functions are Dirichlet-to-Neumann operators of elliptic second-order differential operators. Building upon this analysis, we investigate the convergence rates of the approximation method based on the interpolation operator and establish a dimension-dependent bound for the convergence rates of the approximation method. In the special case where the given operator is the Dirichlet-to-Neumann operator associated with the Laplace operator, we derive dimension-dependent bounds for the convergence rates of various linear approximation methods. In particular, we consider classical Fejér-Hahn's method, the Nystrom method, the Toeplitz representation of the Dirichlet-to-Neumann operator, and others. Ultimately, we provide an explicit estimate for the convergence rates of Fejér-Hahn's method that surpasses the classical Kolmogorov n-width estimates by a significant margin, yielding a dimension-dependent and p- dependent bound. Sgr A East is a radio supernova remnant in the center of the Milky Way that is linked to a massive star explosion occurring within a mill parsec radius radius. This event is believed to have triggered the formation of the compact radio source, G359.95-0.09, and the widespread $10^{49}$ ergs of energy released over a 0.5 parsec radius sphere. Using astrophysical explosion models, our analysis determined the site of the explosion and the motion of the compact radio source. We discovered that the explosion occurred outside the supernova remnant, but within a larger sphere of $10^{49}$ ergs energy. This is consistent with the supernova being associated with the compact radio source and occurring approximately 100 years ago. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that the explosion triggered the formation of the compact radio source and caused the extensive arc-like structure within the supernova remnant. The remnant's energy distribution can be explained by the explosion's impact on the surrounding $40 M_{\odot}$ year 100 gas, forming the eastern arc and the northern ridge. Following the explosion, the dense gas would have triggered the formation of the super star cluster and influenced the surrounding star formation. This is consistent with a peak in star formation occurring approximately 500 years after the explosion triggered by the dense gas. Following the peak, the dense gas would have been dispersed, ending the starburst activity, and the explosion would have triggered the formation of the compact radio source. This is consistent with a 100 year time frame for the explosion to occur between when the starburst activity began and when the compact radio source was detected. The discovery of the explosion's late stage and the early detection of the compact radio source indicates that the explosion is one of the latest stage astrophysical supernovae in the galaxy. These are typically observed as gamma ray bursts. The discovery of the explosion's late stage indicates that there may be a previously undiscovered late stage of a galaxy center supernova, potentially hidden due to the galaxy's dust. The discovery may influence the search for gamma ray bursts in the galaxy's center, increasing the potential for discovering these events, and potentially altering the search parameters for the explosion's earlier stages. As a vital source of public health updates, news influences people's understanding and behavior regarding the outbreak. Research has shown a connection between news coverage and societal responses to the disease. We aimed to explore the relationship between regional news coverage and COVID-19 cases, deaths, and related social media activity in the United States. Employing a data journalism approach, we collected and analyzed data on news coverage, COVID-19 cases, deaths, and related social media activity across 312 regions in the United States from March 2020 to August 2020. They also highlight the need for further research to fully understand the interaction between social media and news coverage and their impact on COVID-19 cases and deaths. The Rapid Multipole Method effectively utilizes multipoole expansion and image point representations to efficiently calculate various physical interactions in distant molecular pairs within N-body simulations. However, when applying this method in literature and codes, the consideration of preserving angular momentum in molecular interactions is often overlooked. Consequently, we derive new equations to ensure angular momentum conservation in the Rapid Multipole Method, involving high-order rotational and orbital moments, and accompanying image points. Specifically, for monomer-based calculations, we present explicit formulas for extracting image points related to these moments and for computing interaction moments via the primary monomer. Furthermore, we provide updated equations for transforming these moments into the laboratory frame, ensuring that these transformations are consistently applied and remove any redundant contributions from the image moments. Notably, when applied to a protein benchmark, the revised algorithm demonstrates superior performance, specifically when compared to a point-to-point method, showing a substantial 5-fold increase in time efficiency while maintaining accurate structural properties. These updated equations and technical insights will significantly enhance the development of future molecular simulation software. The associated source code has been made publicly available and fully integrated with the N-body code, HOmer. By incorporating these new equations, HOmer is now capable of accurately modeling systems that rely on exploiting symmetry to preserve angular momentum. Moreover, our research paves the way for the creation of highly efficient software that balances computational speed and structural precision. For further details on the study, please see our published work at the Journal of Chemical Theory and Modeling, where a more in-depth analysis of the theoretical framework and model development is presented. The related source code can be found through our GitHub page at https://github.com/ho mer-hpc. The HOmer code can be executed with the following command: `make build-mixed` and then running the benchmark with `./ho mer-benchmarks/protein/protein-5000N-ns-SE.cu -d 0`. By disabling image moment optimization via the command line flag `--no-imo-opt`, the protein benchmark can be re-run for comparative purposes. The source code was developed utilizing the CINC environment. The compilation of the code requires an appropriate make build-mer-benchmarks installation. Unveiling these methods allows us to devise a random polynomial-time estimator for the genus of dense graphs. In our analysis, we show that our estimator is efficient, accurate, and robust, yielding results that make sense even in borderline cases. Importantly, the convergence rate of our estimator exceeds the typical speed of dense graph genera by a considerable margin. A detailed examination of our analysis reveals that our methods involve a unique combination of three key components: leveraging tour detection algorithms, exploiting subgraph isomorphism, and employing a precise analysis of a Poisson process applicable to diverse mathematical and computational contexts. Ultimately, our research lays the groundwork for future studies on the statistical properties of various estimation techniques. By combining our analytical approach with Monte-Carlo simulations, we have derived a robust genus estimation algorithm, which yields results consistent with Monte-Carlo simulations. This paper presents a decentralized, asynchronous, and robust approach to solving large-scale convex optimization problems that involve communicating sparse messages among agents over an undirected graph. A single agent, referred to as the master agent, generates random inputs that are disseminated to all other agents, who then use these inputs to calculate gradients, compile the information into a shared pool, and update their individual decision variables through an efficient Newton-like process. By leveraging the sparsity of graph-topology connections, the master agent ensures efficient global gradient computation without exceeding communication limitations. The proposed method has been proven to converge at a linear rate under suitable conditions and withstands a significant range of irregularities in node behavior. Furthermore, it surpasses the performance of comparable methods, such as decentralized gradient descent and decentralized subgradient descent, and also helps to mitigate the impact of unstable behavior. Comprehensive experimental studies validate the theoretical findings by demonstrating the proposed algorithm's ability to solve complex problems efficiently, such as a large-scale multi-asset portfolio optimization problem and a challenging Lasso regression problem. The implementation details, including the choice of time parameters, are discussed in the context of real-world applications. The results show that the proposed algorithm outperforms existing methods, such as the COCO decentralized algorithm and the decentralized Alternating Direction of the Multipliers (DADM) method, by means of both computational efficiency and quality of the solutions produced. As an open contribution to the community, the code used in this research has been made publicly available. The code has been actively employed in several industrial settings, such as the Lasso regression-based production flow control problem at the GE Global Research center and the Lasso-based methods developed by the MIT-IBM Data Science Collaboration to detect non-convex behaviors in cloud-based distributed systems. The code can be accessed at https://github.com/simai-lab/Randomized-Newton-Decentralized-Convex-Optimization. This study examines the detection of hate-speech in two prominent Indo-European languages, Hindi and Bengali, and investigates the effectiveness of various neural network algorithms, including CNN, LSTM and Multi-Layer Perceptron, in classifying hate-speech. The research utilizes the HIBERT model, known for its high performance in English hate-speech detection, to establish a model that can identify hate-speech across languages by adapting it for Hindi and Bengali. The performance of the adapted models and the original HIBERT model, as well as different neural network architectures, is evaluated on two datasets containing hate-speech in Hindi and Bengali, and the study explores the impact of dataset size on model performance. Ammonium sulfate, a ferroelectric and caloric molecular solid with minimal structural changes upon proton transfer, was revisited with new proton relaxation data measured using $^{1}$H magic-angle spinning nuclear magnetic resonance. This new information revealed that in one of its three low-temperature phases, there is a significant proton disorder that persists down to 80 K, contradicting previously suggested order. Incorporating this insight into calculations using the ab initio phonon mode displacement method, it became clear that one particular phase transition out of the four shown in the phase diagram is responsible for the substantial entropy change. According to thermodynamic relationships, the necessary degeneracy for this transition to occur was estimated to be approximately 4.9. Furthermore, using first principles electron density modeling, it was determined that while proton disorder is confirmed upon cooling to 90 K, the resulting high-entropy phase's proton environment remains non-uniform even at 60 K, indicating a more intricate relationship between structural and proton dynamics in this system than previously understood. The analysis highlights the value of further investigating the relationship between structural and proton dynamics in this solid. As robots interact more with people in shared spaces, they need to follow the same rules of behavior that humans do to avoid collisions. We investigated how a person interacts with a robot in a shared environment through a study involving a humanoid manipulator. We found that when working together, a person supervises a robot with planning capabilities to ensure it follows safe paths, which reflects the social norm of avoiding risk. We also observed that when the robot's safety skills improve, it becomes less dependent on the person's supervision, aligning with how humans expect more responsible behavior from other humans. We observed similar responses when the person and robot collaborate on tasks that require understanding intent, such as navigating around obstacles. However, when the person and robot only coexist in the same space, we found that the person does not automatically expect the robot to convey its intentions and may become frustrated if the robot doesn't avoid collisions in a predictable manner. We developed a planning system that allows a robot to suggest person-friendly paths, reducing the chances of errors. This planning system leverages a computational model of human behavior to identify safe paths that minimize disruptions. We validated the effectiveness of this planning system in reducing errors through a large-scale study involving numerous participants. We observed similar results when expanding our findings to various robot shapes and sizes through a simulation-based analysis. Our research opens up new avenues for investigating how shared autonomy can be used to model and promote social norms in collaborative systems. We publicly release the code and data used in our study, enabling others to build upon our work. We discuss the implications of our research on various robot application domains, highlighting areas of future investigation. Furthermore, we explore the broader social context in which our research contributes to understanding multi-agent behavior. We ultimately identify essential properties that autonomous collaborative systems should possess to operate safely and responsibly in shared environments. We discuss the potential benefits and challenges associated with these properties and outline strategies for designing collaborative systems that can effectively communicate with humans in shared spaces. Finally, we explore important research questions and challenges related to the social norms that underlie human-robot collaboration and outline key characteristics that shared autonomous systems should exhibit to operate safely and responsibly in shared environments. We anticipate that our research sparks further investigation into the social and cognitive principles underlying human-robot collaboration and inspire advances in autonomous systems that can effectively communicate with humans in shared spaces. We estimate that our research contributes to understanding human-robot collaboration and designing collaborative systems that can effectively communicate with humans in shared spaces, representing approximately 5 years of effort. In tasks such as robotics and autonomous driving, the ability to effectively navigate complex, unfamiliar environments is crucial, despite familiar places being multi-level in space and organization. Existing navigation methods rely on either global or local spatial knowledge but fail to accommodate a comprehensive understanding of a setting in terms of topology. A new approach to representing layout called HiTMap is presented, incorporating a hierarchical level of organization and topological structure to capture the relationships between different spatial scales and organizational levels. This representation utilizes a modified small-world graph to model cell relationships, taking into account visual consistency across different scales. HiTMap is applied to a variety of applications including 3D mapping and localization, and shows an improvement of 5-10% in navigating through unfamiliar places when compared to existing techniques. Additionally, the proposed method demonstrates an increase of nearly 20% in localization accuracy when compared to existing methods. Experimental results from multiple robotic datasets show HiTMap's ability to effectively scale and improve both navigation and localization capabilities in various settings. Dataset and source code can be found online. Furthermore, the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance in a comparative evaluation of localization techniques using the KITTI dataset KITTI-3D. While slightly outperformed by existing methods in terms of map matching accuracy, when integrated with map-matching techniques, HiTMap shows an improvement of nearly 20% in accuracy. Interestingly, the proposed method shows comparable performance to existing techniques using 3D LiDAR data but shows significantly better results using video data. Video data shows HiTMap outperforming the best existing method by 20% in localization accuracy. A video illustrating HiTMap's performance across multiple scales and organizational levels can be found online. The approach effectively uses multi-modal video data to continuously adapt cell representations to various scales and organizational levels, demonstrating top-notch performance using video data. A future look ahead reveals the potential of integrating HiTMap with graph-based methods for path planning in a multi-scales and organizational hierarchy setting. This research initiative is expected to yield state-of-the-art performance in a variety of applications requiring effective scale and organizational level navigation. Moreover, integrating HiTMap with Map-Matching techniques shows an increase of nearly 20% in localization accuracy, positioning this method to achieve state-of-the-art performance in a variety of applications. A forthcoming publication is expected to present this research initiative. The research program is expected to be extended to a broader array of applications requiring effective scale and organizational level navigation. A key extension to this method involves incorporating HiTMap

Revelation of a nearly imperceptible characteristic of metals at vanishingly small interstitial gaps has sparked excitement for implementing highly localized plasmon-based devices. Electron "spill-over" is a crucial factor influencing plasmon behavior, particularly at narrow gaps, whereas its effect is expected to be negligible at larger gaps. Nevertheless, current electron response theories fail to account for this phenomenon accurately, and prior numerical studies are flawed, neglecting "spill-over" in static calculations and employing an incorrect approximation in dynamic analyses. To address the gap-related electron behavior, we have developed novel nonlocal screening theories, incorporating both exact "spill-over" contributions and an improved approximation for nonlocal screening. Our analysis reveals significant discrepancies between our nonlocal theory and other models, such as DPSS and RPA, particularly in large-gap scenarios, and even reveals an unexpected reversal of the resonance mode at extremely small gaps. Our study demonstrates that nonlocal screening influences plasmon behavior at larger gaps, whereas "spill-over" is crucial in extremely small gaps. This critical assessment enhances our comprehension of plasmon-based phenomena, revealing the necessity to account for both nonlocal screening and "spill-over" in describing gap plasmons. It also underscores that approximations employed earlier have led to incorrect predictions, underscoring the significance of utilizing precise screening theories, especially in describing ultra-small gap behaviors. These findings are anticipated to have a significant impact on designing plasmonic devices, and using precise screening theories is essential to produce reliable outcomes. By comparing quantum simulations (ab initio) and our nonlocal screening theory to the widely utilized DPSS model, we have demonstrated substantial differences in describing surface plasmons at larger gaps. However, our nonlocal screening theory and DPSS model yield comparable results at extremely small gaps, and in describing quasi-bound states within extremely narrow gaps. Our analysis is based on a novel formulation of the electron response that maintains self-consistency and accurately reflects the nonlocal screening and "spill-over" effects. This formulation is set within a general framework, and it is anticipated to be a valuable tool for investigating various screening phenomena and designing nanoscale devices. In various applications like knowledge graph expansion, document summarization, and information retrieval, identifying and disambiguating named entities plays a crucial role. A significant challenge in this process is understanding the context in which an entity's mention is made to determine its specific meaning. One of the entities with the highest mention count, 'UNITED STATES', presents a particular contextuality problem due to its widespread mentions across news, scientific, and web content. To address this issue, we developed a unified pipeline for entity extraction and disambiguation based on a massive aggregated dataset of 'UNITED STATES' entities. We introduced a new entity characteristic called Term Significance, measured as the average frequency ratio of wiki page words versus article words. This approach enables the entity aggregation process to incorporate diverse contexts. By comparing our entity disambiguation tool, called TermSignificant, against three established benchmarks, we found that improved entity context understanding yields, on average, a 2.2% higher F1-score and 0.9% higher precision. Furthermore, our approach outperformed the control groups across six diverse knowledge base construction experiments. The resulting unified pipeline and automatically annotated dataset are now available for research purposes at www.github.com/zhengwenqi/CSF-CMEA, awaiting their eventual integration into production pipelines. The production pipeline incorporating CSF-CMEA achieved deployment on Google's scalable computing infrastructure via Google App Engine. The production data and a related project are accessible via Google Colab, a popular laboratory platform. Displays of time-based data, either individual or collective, are often used in various applications including health, sports, and science. This data type is often viewed as a grid where variables are organized by category and value. In contrast to traditional univariate data, browsing multivariate time-based data involves navigating through combined information of multiple variables, which can be challenging. In response to this difficulty, designers have created visualizations and new viewing techniques to simplify data access and analysis. Nevertheless, accessing specific data points, comparing data, or examining trends across multiple variables often presents difficulties. Conversely, navigating longitudinal data such as growth patterns, is relatively straightforward. This paper proposes a design to simplify navigation and comparison of multivariate time-based data, inspired by longitudinal data approaches. Specifically, we provide a defined vocabulary and set of design principles that enable viewing and interacting with this data type. To validate these principles, we developed an interactive prototype employing high-resolution displays and near-focus optical systems, allowing simultaneous viewing of up to 16 separate time sequences. We then conducted a study with 16 participants to evaluate the effectiveness of this design and obtained positive results, demonstrating incidentally acquired knowledge gains. This research provides valuable insights into simplifying the viewing and interaction of multivariate time-based data. Researchers and developers can utilize the proposed design and various data representation strategies presented here to tackle this data type. This paper also opens the door to further research opportunities, incorporating machine learning methods to automatically suggest meaningful comparisons between data sets. Using a mean-field theory combining Poisson-Boltzmann and mean-spherical model, we analyzed the electric double layer of a charged soft interface surrounded by electrolyte. We derived a comprehensive model of the soft interface's profile and charge density within the electrolyte. We found significant solvent polarization at the soft interface, affecting its interaction with nearby ions. This led to a lower charge density within the electrolyte near the soft interface compared to a hard interface. Furthermore, we investigated the effect of temperature on the electric double layer of the soft interface. We also compared our results to molecular dynamics simulations of a similar system. We discovered that our model's outcomes align well with the simulated results, particularly at low temperatures where the solvent's molecular structure is nearly negligible. However, as temperature rises and the molecular structure of the solvent becomes more prominent, our model's agreement with the simulated results diminishes. This highlights the importance of considering solvent effects in electrical double layer systems, especially at higher temperatures. The knowledge gained from this study can be applied to various systems, such as bio-membranes and nano-particulates in contact with electrolytes. The impact of temperature on these systems may reveal unexpected charge behaviors, underscoring the necessity of a mean-field approach that incorporates solvent effects, particularly at higher temperatures. The study also sheds light on the value of combining theoretical models to better understand the behavior of charged systems in complex environments. The work further advances the concept of charging mechanisms, thereby contributing to a deeper comprehension of the intricacies involved in the charging processes observed in various systems. The study also opens up avenues for exploring the complexities associated with the structural and thermodynamic properties of electrolytes in the vicinity of soft interfaces, potentially leading to a more comprehensive understanding in the future. Research has demonstrated the existence of Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states on individual magnetic adatoms and, more recently, in pairs of magnetic atoms bonded together. Although these pairs are small compared to the wavelength of a spin-polarized quasiparticle on the surface, they still exhibit unique properties. A theoretical model was developed to describe these pairs by reducing a complex Gorkov equation into manageable components. By utilizing recently discovered relationships, the model was implemented for a specific experimental setup involving manganese atoms on a niobium surface. Results showed a significant correlation between the properties of these pairs and the individual properties of each manganese atom as well as their interaction with each other. A notable property of these pairs, the spin-polarized quasiparticle's magnetic field, was found to be directly proportional to the individual manganese atom's properties but inversely related to their interaction. This provides an opportunity to study the characteristics of manganese pairs through analysis of the spin-polarized quasiparticle's magnetic field. Our theoretical model's results are presented for specific manganese pair configurations and compared to an alternative method of prediction. In addition, the model's results for manganese dimers are compared to results from both theoretical models and experimental observations for a relevant experimental setup, with manganese pairs on a niobium surface. Our analysis shows a notable agreement between the results and the available data. Moreover, the model's results for manganese adatoms are used to identify the adatom's orientation for relevant experimental setups. Overall, the model's results demonstrate that manganese pairs on a niobium surface exhibit distinct properties as a function of their relative orientation and the properties of the individual manganese atoms as well as their interaction with each other. These properties are within the range of detection for relevant experimental detection methods. By implementing this model for individual manganese adatoms, the model's results demonstrate that their properties can be distinguished from those of manganese pairs through analysis of the spin-polarized quasiparticle's magnetic field. This provides an opportunity to study the characteristics of individual manganese adatoms using the same detection methods as those used for manganese pairs. In addition, the model's results for manganese pairs reveal that their properties can be varied as a function of the individual manganese atoms as well as their interaction with each other. This provides an opportunity to study the characteristics of these interactions through the analysis of the spin-polarized quasiparticle's magnetic field. This research demonstrates that a wide variety of experimental techniques can be used to study the unique properties of individual manganese adatoms as well

In the vicinity of an absorption edge, the X-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES) exhibits non-linear, complex behavior that is challenging to model. This is due to the intricate two-step process of electronic transitions and the resulting competition between a small number of final-state states. To address this complexity, we introduce the rate framework, a theoretical approach that analyzes the progression of electronic states near an absorption edge by quantifying the relative rates at which electronic systems advance through various states as they undergo multiple-step excitations. By applying this framework to XANES analysis, we can interpret the excitonic characteristics, such as peak positions, widths, and heights, as well as provide insights into the multiple-step excitation process. As an example, we use first-principles calculations to study the 1s-to-p-like resonance in N2, nitrone, and protonated nitrone in a broad energy range that spans approximately 420-440 eV. Our findings demonstrate how the rate framework captures the excitonic characteristics of XANES that are a consequence of a multi-step excitation process, thereby enabling us to make predictions regarding the effects of radiation damage on the stability of delocalized electronic states, particularly those associated with p-block states in nitroza-type molecules. This predictive capability holds significant value for understanding the long-term effects of space radiation on polymers that contain nitrogen, such as those that are used in space blankets. A comprehensive analysis was performed, and results indicate a high degree of accuracy for fully connected networks, as well as notable benefits from reinitializing the network for each subsequent block. The Unigram Coverage (UC) model in Neural Machine Translation (NMT) achieves accurate production by considering the entire target vocabulary. However, its real-time computational cost is significantly high due to the complexity of calculating sentence-level probabilities. This paper presents an alternative approach called the Look-forward Attention for Production (LAP) model, an approximation of the UC model that employs an iterative, forward-looking process to estimate production probabilities in tandem with attention. Notably, LAP's computation time is directly proportional to the number of tokens in the source sentence. Experimental results on the IWSLT'15 and WMT'14 datasets reveal substantial NMT quality improvements, with significant reductions in BLEU score errors. Moreover, LAP surpasses the UC model in both exact and lower-bound metrics while offering a notable increase in decoding speed, ultimately outperforming various state-of-the-art NMT methods. Furthermore, LAP's significant improvements can be applied to other NMT methods, including the Transformer NMT system. Following thorough optimization and analysis, the LAP model is successfully deployed on the Google NMT platform, marking a major milestone in production-ready NMT systems. This research was supported by the US Department of Energy grant number DE-SC0011254. Introduction: This study contributes to understanding the causal structure of diseases and health conditions, leveraging the Philippines' MPHIA dataset. 

Methodology: In this research, we examined the causal connection between health issues using the MPHIA dataset. Traditional structural equation modeling was employed to model the desired relationships. A subset of approximately 6000 samples from the dataset was used for analysis. A grid search approach was utilized to identify the best-fitting parameter values via grid search. A greedy search algorithm was used to determine the optimal causal structure. A covariance matrix was calculated for analysis. A causal structural model was developed, revealing interesting relationships between health conditions. 

Results: The model's model order was identified as 6, supporting a quaternary causal structure. Correlation between health issues was also found, with mental health issues tendentially correlated. 

Conclusion: In conclusion, we established a causal structure among health issues, highlighting their interconnected relationships. These findings may guide policymakers in addressing interconnected health problems. 

In terms of specific health issues, we found a positive correlation between 'Hypertension' and 'Depressive Disorder', indicating that individuals with hypertension are more likely to develop depressive disorder. A negative correlation was found between 'Suicidal Ideation' and 'Mental Health', indicating that mental health contributes negatively to suicidal ideation. 

A subset analysis may be influenced by biases, as indicated by significant correlation values. Nonetheless, these findings may serve as a starting point for further research. 

In addition to the analysis above, we explored other healthcare-related questions using the MPHIA dataset. A model was developed to determine the primary cause of multiple co-occurring health issues. 

Findings revealed a strong causal link between 'Suicidal Ideation' and other health issues, as well as between 'Mental Health' and other health issues. However, 'Depressive Disorder' did not show a significant causal link to other health issues. 

Note that these findings are based on a small sample of the data, and may not be representative of the broader population. 

Ultimately, the purpose of this research is to contribute valuable insights to the understanding of healthcare through data analysis. 

A related question of whether data analysis can be used to understand disease causation remains an open challenge. 

A potential follow-up study involves analyzing the temporal relationship between health conditions. 

Importantly, this research highlights the importance of addressing mental health, as it is closely linked to various other health issues. 

Analysis also reveals the potential causes and correlations of suicidal behavior.

dynamic network algebra models were identified and included in the tool. By

unified approach to model selection. As a result, future research can focus on 
developing certain types of models, such as those based on linear combinations

To address the issue of unauthorized image access, a reversible encryption method is developed to ensure that only authorized parties can decrypt the images. However, since decryption must be impossible for unauthorized parties, standard encryption methods employing random noise are not suitable. Instead, our approach reworks the problem by viewing it as a hidden markov model where the state of the image drives the corresponding noise. Leveraging advances in neural networks and bayesian inference, we create an algorithmic suite that implements this idea. Firstly, a generative neural network model is developed to map image states to their corresponding noise. Following this, a variational neural network is designed to perform state inference by using the noise to make predictions. Both of these networks are trained simultaneously using a novel method. Subsequently, to address potential issues of noise entropy limitations, an extension of the method is developed to allow for more noise configurations. Our approach is tested on various image categories and is found to provide a robust form of concealment that is resistant to both low and high bit rates, while also matching the data rate of current state-of-the-art methods when operating within the same parameters. Our results demonstrate the potential for a range of applications from image to video formats and the ability to achieve successful recovery even in scenarios with significant degradation. Our method is available for public use at https://github.com/adiyoga97/Reversible-Concealment. An accompanying video showcasing the method is available at https://youtu.be/fH8_Hk7Hh4o. This study provides the robust generation of the class of c0-semigroup within a Banach space, leveraging a Lyapunov condition. Building upon the exponential stability of a specific semigroup, we develop a uniformly continuous and exponentially robust semigroup originating from any bounded operator. Our methodology entails Lyapunov conditions posing constraints on the semigroup's generator. Building on previous work by certain authors, who established the relationship between strong stability and robustness, we extend this analysis to the level of c0-semigroups. Our novel findings also include the derivation of the robustness of analytic semigroups and those possessing Hilbert-Schmidt perturbations. Furthermore, we define and explore the notion of robustness within the abstract evolution equations governed by maximal monotone operators, with applications to certain models complemented by a termm of damped elastic-scissor model. Our research provides an extensive review of relevant theories and offers alternative approaches to the concepts of stability and robustness within the dynamically evolving systems. The presented results can be utilized in various real-time applications across control theory, systems biology, medicine, and other fields. The study's numerical examples serve to illustrate the derived results. Ultimately, the presented thesis contributes to the advancement of theories and practical solutions for stability and robustness within complex, multi-faceted systems. This research introduces MuMuPy, a computational program for determining the interaction energies between dimuonium atoms and various substances. Dimuonium is formed from electron-electron interactions that approximately match the energies of ordinary hydrogen atoms. Computed energies utilize variational methods and include corrections for relativity and electronic distribution effects. Users can calculate and estimate interaction energies for dimuonium within substances using given parameters or inputted values for the electronic subspecies distribution. This program is designed to serve as a tool for users looking to calculate dimuonium-substance interaction energies. MuMuPy was developed using Python and is supplemented with a predefined dataset of energies for dimuonium-atom interactions. This work is part of a larger series on dimuonium-substance interactions and a related article on the dimuonium-lead interaction. MuMuPy and additional information are available through the website at muumpy.physics.wm.edu. With MuMuPy, users can efficiently and accurately calculate dimuonium-substance interaction energies. Calculation examples are provided, covering a range of substances from noble gases to complex materials like tungsten and lead, illustrating the program's functionality. Effective content summarization is crucial for coping with information overload, and it's particularly challenging when dealing with lengthy documents with low signal words. Machine learning-based approaches can excel in identifying key points from vast datasets, but they sometimes struggle with specific tasks involving special forms of text like poetry, where the relationship between words and content is intricate. Human-created summaries, on the other hand, aim to capture a deeper understanding of the original material, however relying solely on human summarization is impractical due to time constraints and the costs associated.

Platforms such as Amazon's Mechanical Turk allow researchers to tap into a large pool of content workers, yet there's a significant risk involved in hiring unqualified workers who may not possess the necessary language proficiency and reading comprehension skills to effectively understand and summarize complex content. Our study focuses on the efficiency of MTurk-based human summarization by developing and evaluating a multi-faceted filtering system for identifying and hiring qualified workers. We discovered that combining workers' performance with specific tasks using high-accuracy text recognition and reading comprehension tests, in addition to evaluating their summarization skills and assessing their linguistic proficiency using standardized tests, is key to achieving a reliable human summarization system. Furthermore, by implementing a rigorous filtering process, researchers can identify and recruit qualified MTurk workers who can deliver high-quality summaries, outperforming machine learning-based competitors in terms of content coverage and understanding, as seen across a series of experiments and case studies involving various types of low signal-rich documents including news articles, scholarly content, and a subset of poetry, ultimately resulting in a near-optimal summarization performance, rivaling that of human professionals. Our proposed solution is freely available on our GitHub repository, including the source code, allowing for easy adaptation and use in other settings. We believe that establishing a robust and efficient human summarization pipeline has the potential to revolutionize the field and cater to a wide array of challenging document types. Importantly, our research highlights the importance of accurately identifying qualified content workers as a critical component of content-based MTurk projects, and showcases how a multi-faceted filtering process can effectively locate and hire workers possessing exceptional language skills, thereby unlocking their full potential as content experts. Our findings have significant implications across a variety of domains including content analysis, search, natural language processing, and recommendation systems, and could easily be adapted and extended to address other difficult content creation tasks, ultimately paving the way for significant breakthroughs in the adjacent fields of content generation, extraction, and discovery. Our model can potentially be applied to other project crowdsourcing initiatives

Text-video retrieval, an essential task of practical importance, requires matching video content with text data. To improve performance, researchers have been developing sophisticated models, but many current approaches still rely on outdated architectures. Specifically, older models' feature extractors were separate, making it difficult to incorporate their insights into further processing. To overcome these limitations, a new method, TS2-Net, was developed. This approach integrates both text and video encoders into a single model, allowing token shifting and selection to enhance the quality of extracted features. Neural network performance is typically enhanced through larger architectures,
but this leads to significantly longer training times as network size increases.
A major training challenge arises from the network's ability to process vast amounts
of input data, which can overwhelm the regularized loss and cause convergence issues
during the optimization process. Our new method, Sparsity Differentiable Regularized
Neural Networks (SDRNN), addresses these concerns by defining expressible sparsity measures
and a conveyance function to quantify data processing complexity. Constrained by a limited
number of active parameters, neural networks can now be trained efficiently with reduced
size, achieving better performance, or with the same size, achieving faster training times.
Our experiments show that SDRNN surpasses existing methods in sparsity metrics while achieving
higher accuracy, or faster convergence, than using sparsity measures alone. Moreover,
SDRNN enables automatic determination of the optimal number of active parameters, unshackling
the potential of neural architecture search from the previous limitations. Using SDRNN, we
successfully train ResNet-205, achieving a higher accuracy than the previously thought best model,
ResNet-200, with only half as many parameters, or equal, as previously thought necessary.

We establish that the constructed models possess well-defined global invariants, namely, the distance between sets involved in the sweeping process and the moving trajectories. Moreover, by employing suitable monotone operator theory, we prove the existence and stability of periodic solutions for these composite models under substantially relaxed conditions. To achieve this, we first introduce novel, structural hypotheses for the involved moving convex compact sets. These new assumptions encompass a broad range of set variations and reduce to existing, standardized conditions for specific types of moving sets. Ultimately, as a practical application of our findings, we investigate and analyze a class of mechanical models with applications to rigid and flexural bodies, detailing specifically the dynamics of a rigid body sliding onto a wedge and the longitudinal oscillations of a van der Pol-type pendulum, all within the presence of Coulomb friction and a rotating frame of reference. Lastly, a thorough simulation study is conducted to verify the theoretical results, produce solution approximations, and provide a means to quantify the effect of experimental and modeling errors. This research contributes to the development of a sweeping-type integral-differential model, a more comprehensive mechanical model, and a novel approach to analyzing periodic solutions in a more general model format. This research paper focuses on resolving the Nirenberg problem, specifically for metric geometries on the half-sphere. Uncovering a non-trivial solution requires developing an intricate deformed metric from a given metric $g_f$, which describes a constant negative curvature on a two-dimensional sphere. Unfolding the analysis, it becomes apparent that non-trivial solutions appear only when certain conditions are met regarding the Lichnerowicz method and the Lott-Villamizar-Hulin methods, which include leveraging a deformed metric with an inherent Ricci curvature. Moreover, studying critical points from both Lichnerowicz and Lott-Villamizar-Hulin methods, as well as analyzing their relationships with Euler characteristics, leads to a broader understanding of the problem. Ultimately, combining these observations with a more refined approach to solving the Nirenberg problem, which takes into account metric geometries on the half-sphere, yields a non-trivial solution, which has been verified with a Lichnerowicz eigenfunction as well as through a more detailed analysis of the Lott-Villamizar-Hulin method. A particularly significant metric geometry on the half-sphere, which supports a non-trivial solution, can be achieved by implementing a blow-up strategy of the deformed metric. Moreover, demonstrating the appearance of a non-trivial solution when using blow-up on the half-sphere, following the Lott-Villamizar-Hulin method, leads to a more complete understanding of the problem at hand. A new method for learning deep representations is introduced, focusing on dimensionality reduction. Unlike traditional techniques such as AutoEncopes, the novel approach targets a more optimal solution by minimising the Wasserstein distance between original and compressed data. Although challenging to calculate, a theoretical connection between Wasserstein distance and a method called Sinkhorn distances is established. A related loss function, known as Sinkhorn loss, is then formulated and incorporated into a deep learning framework. A series of experiments were conducted to evaluate the novel approach, comparing its performance to established methods like PCA, t-SNE and other non-supervised deep learning techniques. The results show the new method outperforms or matches existing algorithms in data compressions, particularly with a study involving 100,000 vectors. A related demonstration tool is available online. 

Key words: Deep learning, dimensionality reduction, Wasserstein distance, Wasserstein loss, Sinkhorn loss, unsupervised learning.

In the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, a pivotal question arises regarding the applicability and enhancement of contact tracing methods. In England, local tracing collaborations played a significant role in the efforts to contain COVID-19, yet the impact of collaborative efforts remains unclear. We investigated the influence of these local collaborations on the success of contact tracing during the pandemic. Our study covered 19 regional collaborations across England, focusing on nearly 70% of cases between July 2021 and June 2022. We employed Bayesian sequential analysis to assess whether the collaborations accelerated case finding, improved the average number of case-line contacts identified per case, and influenced the average number of case-line contacts that were successfully contacted and self-isolated. Our findings indicated that the collaborations increased the daily average of case-line contacts identified by 10-30%, although no significant effect was found on case finding or the proportion of case-line contacts contacted. Notably, the analysis revealed that the collaborations enhanced daily case finding by up to 5%. We discovered considerable variation in the collaborations' performance, suggesting opportunities for improvement in areas such as information sharing, data analysis, and efficiency in adding new case-line contacts for investigation. Our study's findings are likely transferable to other contact tracing initiatives, particularly those focused on COVID-19 or future infectious disease outbreaks. It is anticipated that similar analysis will be essential for evaluating the success of future local tracing collaborations, enabling data-driven decisions regarding the continuation or modification of collaborative efforts. Moreover, our study offers a framework for assessing the impact of other local tracing initiatives on the success of contact tracing during the COVID-19 pandemic and future outbreaks. The evaluation of musical compositions has been a centuries-long practice spanning both positive and negative outcomes. Historically, human evaluation relied on expert musical knowledge, but the growing prevalence of artificial intelligence (AI) composition tools demands an objective evaluation method. Our proposed approach uses advanced AI models, specifically effective transformer-language models, to evaluate compositions both quantitatively and objectively. By adapting and employing computational techniques from natural language processing, this method recognizes, interprets, and analyzes the structural elements of music. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses others in both accuracy and speed. Moreover, when combined with a composition generative system, our method enables both composition and evaluation of musical works. Our study also includes a comprehensive analysis of the limitations and potential applications of this method, including its implications for understanding musical preferences and the nature of beauty in musical compositions. Ultimately, our AI-powered evaluation method successfully addresses the challenge of objective musical composition evaluation. Our source code is freely available for researchers on GitHub at https://github.com/isl-nc3/AIEvaluation.

Our proposed method, Box Re-Ranking (BRR), employs an efficient and novel approach to eliminate false positives in object detection. By integrating re-ranking with rich component-based information, BRR reduces the need for costly network modifications, domain adaptation, or hard example mining. Our method simplifies this task by directly comparing the detected box scores with a user-defined threshold, rather than competing scores. This results in an unsupervised method that achieves comparable performance to supervised techniques. Our experiments show BRR achieves a 73.6% false alarm rate reduction on the CROWDSURF benchmark, outperforming state-of-the-art methods. Our code is publicly available on GitHub. With BRR, we set a new unsupervised benchmark on CROWDSURF with an average AP of 64.9, significantly improving the previous unsupervised average AP of 45.7. Our method also surpasses state-of-the-art supervised methods when integrated with weakly supervised bounding box re-ranking techniques. This work is a comprehensive analysis of Box Re-Ranking on the CROWDSURF benchmark, offering a new benchmark and extensive analysis. An accompanying video details our findings. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/asharakeh/box-re-ranking. Our primary objective is to understand the impact of incorrect simulation of throwing motions on viewer trust in the character's actions. To achieve this, we created a web-based experiment where participants viewed sequences of animations depicting characters throwing objects. Each sequence featured either a correct or an artificially manipulated trajectory, derived from captured human throwing data. We instructed the participants to state whether they believed the character had intentionally thrown the object and whether they thought the character was skilled in throwing. The results revealed that even minor distortions in the character's throwing motion can lead viewers to doubt the character's intentions and skill level. Notably, this suggests that excessive realism in the simulation may be detrimental in contexts involving intentional character actions. Our study also implies that validating character abilities through non-verbal cues (such as the trajectory of the object) can be ineffective due to the influence of realistic simulations and the complexity of processing mental states. Furthermore, we observed a connection between specific arm and object interactions (such as the ball's trajectory) and the perception of the character's skill level. Interestingly, this relationship did not apply to perceived intentional behavior. Ultimately, our research offers insights into the design of more realistic and engaging characters in virtual environments by investigating the impact of simulated throwing motions on human perception. The experiment's data and results are publicly available online. Based on these findings, we propose several guidelines for authors and developers to create more convincing and intelligent character animations. Ultimately, our research aims to understand the delicate balance between achieving high levels of realism in character animations and ensuring that character behaviors align with reasonable human expectations. Our study presents an efficient approach to approximate Hamiltonian spectra by leveraging random Clifford circuits of moderate complexity. These circuits are feasible to compute classically within existing time constraints. Their depth can be kept shallow, allowing for an unaffiliated running time, unaffected by the circuit size, which is a crucial factor in their implementation. When tested on well-known Hamiltonians, our protocol showed results comparable to the best current protocols, but its utility lies primarily in its ability to provide accurate information for complex, yet hard-to-simulate quantum systems. Notably, our work supplements a recent experiment by solving a distinct puzzle involving the same models. In addition to the proposed shallow shades protocol, we've also developed an advanced version of the shades of gray approach, which builds upon previous work and yields finer spectral estimates. The new protocol is grounded in the application of multi-qubit entangling gates in a controlled environment. Based on the findings from our shallow shades protocol using low-depth circuits, we've obtained new bounds for the shades of gray approach, leading to a finer estimate of the spectral variation for an eight-spin model based on the trace of its partial transpose. The new bound is roughly 25 percent better than a comparable previous estimate. Our work on these shallow shades and advanced shades of gray approaches highlights their potential for coexistence, allowing for the application of different protocols to different regions of the Hamiltonian's spectrum, thereby refining the estimates and bringing the results closer together. Ultimately, our study's conclusions are reinforced by comparisons between the spectral properties of specific models, including an eight-spin model based on the trace of its partial transpose and a model representing two levels of an anharmonic oscillator. In the case of the anharmonic oscillator model, our study's findings are supported by the analytical solution to the problem, while the eight-qubit model serves as a comprehensive test of the efficiency and performance of the proposed protocols. These studies and conclusions lay the groundwork for future quantum phase estimation experiments, paving the way for the application of these techniques to the estimation of Hamiltonian spectra. The Sibyl dataset, comprising obfuscated English text categories, poses significant difficulties for unsupervised categorization tasks. To address this challenge, we investigated various transformations in both 2D and hand-writing formats with the aim of making text more readable for machines while preserving its original semantic value, ultimately facilitating better categorization results. From an analytical perspective, we evaluated the effects of these transformations on both the visual and textual aspects of individual characters. Our findings revealed that certain modifications, although imperceptible to humans, can be detected by machines. To counter this, we introduced a new set of transformations, dubbed sibylvarants, which are designed to confuse both human vision and machine algorithms. Through our experiments, we identified the most effective set of transformations that enhance machine readability, as well as the benefits of combining multiple schemes within a robust 1-nearest-neighbor classifier. Notably, the proposed method achieved an impressive accuracy of 53.16%, representing a substantial improvement of over 19% compared to a baseline high-entropy scheme (33.53%), and a considerable gain of more than 13% over another top-performing transformation, "zer0" (39.73%). Furthermore, we observed that the sibylvariant method performed competitively when applied to an alternative high-accuracy dataset, LSA. The proposed approach and associated data sets are made freely available for further research and development purposes. A key advantage of our approach is the transparent nature of these algorithms, allowing for easy verification, whereas the processes underlying deep learning models are shrouded in ambiguity. Focusing on linear models, we have created two frameworks: one based on projection and another driven by data transformation. When paired with a suitable objective function, such as contrastive learning, our methods can teach the linear model to effectively represent complex inputs in a straightforward, high-dimensional context. Furthermore, our methods can be adapted for incremental learning, enabling the linear model to adapt to new classes with minimal effort. A major concern with these approaches, however, lies in their stability and reliability. In this paper, we assess the consistency and effectiveness of Quantization and Extraction methods in low-resource MT models, with a focus on improving model efficiency. Our analysis delves into the impact of parameter weight distribution and suggests novel strategies to enhance the robustness of these methods. Experimental results demonstrate that while some approaches prove stable and efficient in the majority of cases, they can also result in significant performance drops in specific scenarios. Based on our findings, we provide recommendations for optimizing the application of Quantization and Extraction methods to models such as translation. Ultimately, our study aims to lay the groundwork for a more thorough evaluation of these methods and to stimulate further research in the development of Lightweight Low-Resource MT models. The code used in this research will be made publicly available. Notably, the MICTA dataset is one of the first to feature augmented X-ray images to demonstrate the effectiveness of augmented data in medical image processing. This research aims to explore whether additional, unlabelled data – sourced from uninfected patients and enriched with image processing techniques – can further boost detection accuracy. Intelligent systems are relied upon for critical decision-making in various emergency situations. For example, autonomous robots working in hazardous environments need to be protected from harm. Consequently, understanding cause-and-effect relationships between actions and damage becomes vital for developing and deploying these systems effectively. Moreover, accurately modeling cause-and-effect in such scenarios is necessary for teaching intelligent systems to make informed decisions. Therefore, we collected a substantial dataset consisting of 33,000 scenarios depicting damage instances in 3D environments and the events that led to them. Our analysis of this data involves the dependences among variables, the correlation of variables, and the causal inquiry through question-answering. Our research reveals that quantitatively measuring variables such as size, orientation, and composition of objects, and environmental factors like terrain and weather, can significantly contribute to predicting damage causes. Furthermore, we observed that objects and environments are associated with similar causal properties. Additionally, we found that some objects and environments share common causal properties, likely due to their geometric and compositional similarities. From our model, we identified and excluded illogical causes of damage, such as objects causing other objects or vice versa. Our results also point out inconsistencies in the data, such as a shot arrow potentially causing damage to multiple objects. These findings indicate that damage causes can be accurately modeled, thus enabling autonomous systems to effectively avoid harm and learn from experience. Our dataset and models are available for public use, marking a significant step in the development of causal knowledge for intelligent systems. Our work has been successfully applied in other areas for generating damage-causing scenes and designing autonomous robots to complete tasks safely. Our model's effectiveness has been tested in several studies, such as its initial publication in 2020, as well as various subsequent studies in 2021. A related video is also available for further reference. Information about potential issues with the model's generalizability can also be found. Suggestions for future research can be found in the supplementary material. Relevant code can be found at https://github.com/tonyiu/damage-cycles. Recent advancements in end-to-end speech-to-speech translation have been substantial but still fall short in two key areas: the need for extensive training datasets and a limited range of language pairs they can handle.  This research addresses these challenges by exploring zero-shot and few-shot approaches to speech translation through the use of zero-shot speech translation models that require no manual training for each language pair.  By reorganizing the speech translation task into two separate steps: speech translation via transcription, and transcription-based translation, it becomes possible to leverage pre-existing translation and transcription models, and further adapt these models to accommodate speech translation by fine-tuning them using masked LM objectives.  Our studies conducted on the MuST-c dataset reveal that the zero-shot approach to speech translation can achieve a score of 5.0 BLEU when using German as the source language and English as the target language, a significant improvement over the baseline LM alone.  Moreover, by utilizing a pre-trained German-English translation model and adapting it to the speech translation task, we were able to boost the score to 9.5 BLEu when the source language is German and the target language English.  This breakthrough score significantly closes the gap between the score achieved through speech-to-speech translation models and that achieved through speech-to-text and text-to-text models.  Our research also demonstrates that the approach to adapting the LMs used in this study is versatile and can be used to facilitate speech translation in any language pair by starting with the most advanced LMs that have been fine-tuned on translation tasks.  This development marks a major step forward in the development of speech translation systems, and it represents a significant shift away from the current reliance on speech-to-speech translation models, and towards systems that leverage fine-tuned LMs that require little or no manual adjustment for each language pair.  Our study also shows that the approach to adapting the LMs used in this study can also be used to facilitate the task of speech translation when initiated only with translation models, and it requires no manual adjustment for the speech transcription step. This work introduces extensions to the Coleman-Gurtin type equations, incorporating boundary conditions that respond dynamically to the thermodynamic fluxes and temperature. We focus on theories with linear relaxation, ensuring the interior and boundary energy densities decrease over time. By embedding a nonlinear diffusion mechanism within a finite region, we observe that the interior and boundary energies eventually converge to a uniform equilibrium state under certain conditions. Multi-dimensional solutions exhibiting spatially inhomogeneous patterns are also constructed, and we establish the global and local well-posedness of the system through a fixed-point argument, even in the presence of small diffusion. Furthermore, the behavior of multi-dimensional solutions in a compact domain is studied as the size of the domain approaches zero. We discover that the solutions may converge to a traveling wave that resides on the boundary, or they may experience a transition from a non-trivial state to a uniform equilibrium state over time, and we establish the theoretical justification for this phenomenon through a singular limit argument. Specifically, we demonstrate the existence of solutions that reside partially or entirely on the boundary by considering a singularly perturbed version of the boundary condition, and we obtain an asymptotic analysis that reveals the limiting equation governing the boundary behavior. A comparison principle for the boundary temperature reveals that it must be non-negative and must satisfy a nonlinear diffusion equation, and we observe that the solutions may exhibit a variety of behaviors, such as spatially constant or inhomogeneous states, by considering a variety of limiting equations and boundary conditions. By establishing the uniqueness of the asymptotic solution and the behavior of the transition front, we complete our analysis of the theory, and our work provides a comprehensive understanding of the behavior of the Coleman-Gurtin type equations, especially in the context of the non-standard boundary conditions. Moreover, our work reveals that the theory possesses a wide range of possibilities for the design and modeling of spatially inhomogeneous or dynamic structures, and we provide a theoretical justification for the observed phenomena through a fixed-point argument, the singular limit argument and the comparison principle for the boundary temperature. Finally, our work highlights the utility of the theory as a mathematical framework for the modeling and analysis of thermodynamic systems with dynamic boundaries. Forecasting consumption in low voltage networks is particularly demanding due to the lack of detailed measurement data, making it necessary to leverage forecasts from other network levels to fill this gap. This study explores how using sub-hourly consumption forecasts, which are typically available at the medium and high voltage levels, can help improve low voltage forecast accuracy. To address limitations in forecast precision, probabilistic forecasting techniques are introduced, allowing for the improvement of aggregate consumption forecasts at both individual and combined low voltage feeders. Using data from 28, 15-minute measured feeders and high-resolution forecasts, the benefits of merging forecasts and increasing forecast resolution are quantitatively assessed, ultimately demonstrating how these approaches can reduce the mean absolute error (MAE) of individual feeders by 19%. To gain a deeper understanding of these improvements, a data analysis is performed, focusing on the characteristics of successful predictions, the sources of inaccuracy, and notable consumption peaks, which are found to be closely linked to high consumption values, highlighting the necessity for near-real-time feedback loops between the network levels to efficiently coordinate distribution systems. Following peak consumption periods, the sudden changes in consumption patterns often caught high-resolution forecasts off guard, underscoring the value of near-real-time communication, while the analysis also revealed that around 40% of the identified errors occurred during periods of increased consumption, emphasizing the need for more precise forecasts outside typical consumption patterns. To overcome these limitations, the integration of smart meters equipped with load controllers, which can respond to sudden changes in consumption, is proposed, enabling the reduction of uncertainty during peak hours, which could be particularly beneficial during events like consumer lunches or pre-cooling hours. Additionally, the analysis of forecast inaccuracy showed that errors were more likely to occur during periods of increased consumption, underscoring the necessity for more precise forecasts outside typical consumption patterns. To mitigate these precision problems, the integration of smart meters capable of load control is proposed, which can respond to consumption changes, ultimately reducing uncertainty during peak hours, which could be particularly beneficial during events like consumer lunches or pre-cooling hours. Ultimately, the analysis indicates that the combination of high-resolution forecasts, the increase of forecast resolution, the integration of external forecasts, and the analysis of consumption patterns and peak events are all crucial for improving low voltage feeders' consumption forecasts. To address remaining challenges, the development of real-time communication networks and the integration of responsive resources like demand response, energy storage, and load management are proposed, which can enhance the resilience and efficiency of distribution systems by enabling them to adapt to consumption patterns

The integration of domain expertise in machine learning is crucial for delivering accurate results. While some domain experts are familiar with the process, many are unaware of how their input affects model development and validation, making it difficult to interpret outcomes. Furthermore, domain experts typically lack in-depth knowledge of the underlying problem, its underlying principles, and relevant theoretical concepts. As a result, their input is usually confined to labeling data. But what specific features should they highlight? How can they influence the choice of models and evaluation methods? We outline a step-by-step framework for incorporating domain expertise at every stage of the machine learning process. The guide focuses on image analysis tasks, but concepts are easily applicable to other domains as well. By following this structure, readers can tailor the advice to their specific needs. The goal of this document is to provide a comprehensive overview of the roles and responsibilities involved in machine learning, promoting collaboration and understanding between domain experts and machine learning professionals. By working together, they can achieve more effective domain integration. A collaborative GitHub repository at https://github.com/teamlab-ucsb/blueprint-domain-expertise contains the necessary materials for implementing the suggested framework. The repository includes a step-by-step guide for integrating domain expertise, along with the data used to develop the evaluated models, the employed evaluation metrics, and the corresponding results. The goal is to facilitate replication and facilitate domain expertise integration. The final version of this document is publicly available at https://teamlab.ucsb.edu/blueprint-domain-expertise. The original work was completed in June 2021.
