The current methods for detecting COVID-19 lesions are biased and rely on specific assumptions about the appearance of the lungs and LULs in chest CT scans. However, COVID-19 is a new disease and we still don't know how its lesions look, which makes it difficult for existing models to accurately identify them. To overcome this limitation, we propose the Weakly Guided Learning for Detecting COVID-19 Lesions (W2D-CL) framework, which can accurately locate LULs in chest CT scans without making any assumptions about their appearance. By using lung masks to mask the entire image except for the lungs, we convert the difficult task of detecting LULs into an easier task of segmenting the lungs and locating LULs within them. Our model consists of two stages, the first stage identifies LUL candidate regions based on low resolution images and the second stage refines these candidates based on the original image, thereby improving accuracy. By adjusting the size of the LULs, we can control the precision of the first stage, which is beneficial in reducing false positives in the second stage. Our model was evaluated using the EmoLUL dataset and outperformed all existing competition, specifically improving the average F1-score by 8.1% compared to the current best model. Additionally, we observed a high F1-score of 76.9% for false LULs that were present in 12% of the images, indicating our model's ability to accurately identify LULs that weren't actually present in the images. To the best of our knowledge, this framework provides the most accurate detection of COVID-19 lesions to date. Accurate vertebral body identification is crucial in various medical applications such as fracture detection and spinal alignment assessment. This task becomes more difficult when using common 2D or 3D image processing techniques due to limitations such as partial vertebral fractures or limited field of view. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a novel, fully automatic 3D CT scan analysis approach that recognizes and counts vertebral bodies in the upper and lower parts of the spine, despite fractures or limited scans. This innovative method uses spine rectification to effectively separate and organize scan fragments based on vertebral characteristics, followed by a comprehensive, constrained optimization process to precisely locate and recognize each vertebral body in three-dimensional space. By integrating distinct vertebral features, this approach can accurately identify and distinguish vertebral bodies, even when fractured or scanned partially. To ensure anatomical feasibility, it includes constraints based on anatomical spacing between vertebral bodies. By relying on distinctive vertebral characteristics rather than fractures or scan limitations, this approach can accurately and robustly identify and count vertebral bodies, making it suitable for various research and clinical applications. To demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of our technique, we applied and tested it on a large collection of 350 CT scans, featuring 70-100 vertebral bodies each, as part of the Osteoporosis Cure CT research project. This approach identified and counted vertebral bodies with 100% accuracy and assessed fracture presence with 98% accuracy. These results represent the most accurate and robust outcomes to date, exceeding previous performance benchmarks. To facilitate future research, we have made our approach available as an open-source software tool. This resource, known as SpineLoc, can be used by researchers and clinicians to accurately and automatically analyze spine fractures and other spinal abnormalities in CT scans. SpineLoc represents the first open-source high-performance, automatic, 3D CT scan analysis approach to recognize and count vertebral bodies, further enabling the fracture detection and other various medical and research applications. To date, it significantly surpasses existing solutions by providing more accurate and robust outcomes. This resource is expected to greatly contribute to future research, particularly in the field of fracture detection and other medical and spinal-related applications. To make this software accessible to a broader range of users, we have also created a companion video that provides step-by-step guidance and demonstrates its key features. Researchers are developing extremely powerful light sources that can encircle and energize tiny particles with an enormous amount of energy. By trapping these powerful light sources within an incredibly tiny space, they can achieve previously unimaginable levels of energy and interaction. In this research, we demonstrate that an energy-storing light environment can prevent particles from losing their energy and may even boost it beyond its initial levels. We've identified a specific mechanism, electron scattering, that occurs when powerful light interacts with delicate systems in a highly confined space. An interaction that typically causes energy loss can become a source of energy gain in this specific mechanism. We've demonstrated that this energy-gaining process can be triggered and controlled both externally and internally. Together with theoretical models and mathematical simulations, we show that this new energy-gaining process can open up new pathways for scientists to develop stable and energized materials. In fact, we've found that this new process is so favored that it becomes the dominant interaction at an extremely high level of energy release. In this study, we've used a specific interaction between electrons and photons to develop a new energy-gaining process that can be used to stabilize and energize materials. We've shown that it becomes the dominant interaction at an extremely high level of energy release. This new energy-gaining process has a wide range of potential applications in various fields, including the development of stable and energized materials and novel light-based interactions. The versatility of elastic actuators (EA) in legged robot designs has piqued the interest of researchers. Compared to traditional position-controlled actuators, elastic actuators possess several benefits, such as decreased weight, improved factorization of efforts, and enhanced energy absorption capabilities. Leveraging these advantages during daily tasks can significantly increase a quadruped robot's efficiency. To effectively utilize EA-based actuators, a new method that integrates maximum-casualty model learning is presented in this study. This model acknowledges the limitations of current elastic actuator models and learns the most critical elements for a specific movement, as well as the optimal way to decompose forces and energies. Model learning is demonstrated on a Cassie model-based quadruped robot equipped with various elastic actuators in its legs, limbs, and back. Our findings show that specific EA models can significantly boost the robot's endurance by 2.8 to 4.7 times, and models learned from one task can also be applied to others. Furthermore, our research emphasizes the importance of recognizing and accounting for energy storage and absorption during the development and utilization of EA models. The research outcomes and findings are expected to pave the way for future research directions and applications. Understanding the small-scale tearing instability is essential for modeling earth's edge-dispersed magnetic particles and volcanic eruptions, as well as other plasma phenomena. Prior research indicated that microscale tearing in slab plasamas typically requires unrealistically high levels of external driving force. Subsequent studies found that a localized force can trigger the instability, but did not provide a comprehensive framework for analyzing the effect. Our in vitro experiments and accompanying simulations reveal that a localized drive can indeed trigger the instability, and show that the subsequent growth of the tearing mode is influenced by the external drive's intensity and pattern. Additionally, our experiments and simulations suggest the existence of a scaling law for predicting the instability's growth rate, and identify key parameters that govern the growth rate and stability. Notably, our findings indicate that the drive's characteristics can significantly impact the tearing mode's behavior, and suggest that a partial correlation function provides a more accurate description of the drive's effect on the stability than a simple peak value. Our research further indicates that accounting for spatial variations in the drive yields improved agreement between simulations and experiments. Overall, our experiments and simulations provide new insights into the small-scale tearing instability and demonstrate the value of combining experimental and simulation methods for gaining a deeper understanding of this instability and its implications for various systems, including geophysical and geological plasmas. As such, our work has significant potential for advancing knowledge and understanding of these complex systems, and for enabling more accurate modeling and prediction of their behavior. Our research further indicates that an energy-based stability criterion can be used to describe the small-scale tearing instability and its performance in simulations and experiments, and provides a new perspective on the microscale tearing instability and its characteristics. We expect that our research will significantly contribute to the development of realistic and accurate models for describing this instability and its effects in various systems, and for advancing our understanding of this important phenomenon. We conclude by highlighting the significance of interdisciplinarity in this research and its potential for enabling further breakthroughs at the intersection of plasma physics and geophysics and geology. This research focuses on utilizing trait-based fashion search, distinguishing it from standard image retrieval approaches. A key challenge arises from the lack of data and the requirement to define traits, which are essential features in this field. Existing methods are unsuitable for this application due to their reliance on comprehensive annotations. A new framework, FABRIK, addresses these issues by introducing a feature-level attribute manipulation technique utilizing generative models and a novel reconstruction-based framework. Evaluations conducted on the FashionGenere dataset and the PAIR dataset highlight FABRIK's superior performance in retrieving relevant items, and its ability to accurately identify items consistent with specified traits. Notably, FABRIK achieves accurate results with limited or no definitions of the traits provided, and with minimal required annotations, which are simply the target traits themselves. FABRIK's design allows for real-time search functionality, and it can be used to suggest items consistent with particular traits as well as to recommend changes to existing outfits to create more desirable combinations of traits. Furthermore, FABRIK demonstrates its ability to handle unlabelled data during training, and this semi-supervised nature significantly reduces the required amount of annotations. Overall, FABRIK's semi-supervised semi-join ranking algorithm and feature-level trait manipulation functionality make it a vital component in fashion search applications. In practice, it enhances user experience by suggesting relevant search queries and outfit recommendations. A live demo of FABRIK is available at a live website. 

Key related contributions of this research are outlined below.

1.  A novel semi-supervised algorithm is proposed for attribute-level manipulation, and it significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches by maintaining accuracy while significantly reducing required annotations by 40%.
2.  A new reconstruction-based framework, requiring no image synthesis, is developed for attribute-level manipulation. Consequently, it does not degrade image retrieval metrics such as recall and average precision, and it does not require retraining when changing the attribute definitions.
3.  A semi-supervised algorithm is proposed for attribute-level manipulation, and it achieves accurate results with definitions of the attributes provided but also with limited and no definitions provided as required for training.
4.  A live demo of FABRIK is available at a live website. 

These outcomes and methods, and in particular the live demo of FABRIK, will likely be of considerable interest to researchers, practitioners and readers.  Key words: Fashion search, semi-supervised attribute-level manipulation, semi-supervised join ranking, fashion genere, pair datasets

The existing methods for solving ill-posed problems, such as Tikhonov method, carry the risk of discarding important solution features to minimize noise. To mitigate this, we develop an algorithm which preserves key features of the solution. Our proposed algorithm uses dual gradients to determine optimal parameters for the solution's hyperparameters. In a typical setting, we minimize regularization parameters' impact on the solution. To prove our algorithm's effectiveness, we first establish the convexity of the dual objective in an abstract Banach space, then analyze the convergence of the algorithm in a K-convex smooth setting, and verify the feasibility of the method in a practical scenario involving 1-dimensional linear equations. Our results are further supported by the results of a real-world experiment, which shows the potential of the method to retain important features of the solution, and highlights its differences from the Tikhonov method. To validate the performance of the method, we compare it to the Tikhonov method and contemporary neural network-based methods, such as DeepIPSCN, which only works for 2D or 3D matrices. Our study also identifies potential areas of improvement for the method. The presented research builds upon our previous work, and is further supplemented by a provided Matlab code for the method, as well as the used datasets, and ground truth values, and plots of the study. A novel, deep learning-based approach has been developed for light field depth estimation called the Occlusion-Aware Cost Generator (OACG). This method uniquely shifts cost calculation from each pixel's relative depth to each pixel's epipolar slice relative depth, thereby decreasing computation and enhancing real-time capability. In contrast to prior methods, OACEG's cost calculation avoids the angular ambiguity of constant-depth regions by introducing a tight lower limit to the cost, made possible by leveraging the concept of constant-q quads and identifying the minimum cost based on a 4-point parallax. Furthermore, OACEG's cost calculation avoids the pitfalls of fake stationary points arising from occlusion, while its lower bound ensures smooth local depth inference free from their interference. As a result, in areas where a point isoclinic's depth remains constant, OACEG's cost is predominantly comprised of the point's epipolar slice cost, thereby yielding superior real-time light field depth estimation performance. The proposed approach outperforms existing methods on the standard "buddha" light field benchmark by approximately 0.5% and demonstrates significant real-time capabilities by running at 30-40 FPS on an NGCNV3D GPU. The full implementation can be found at https://github.com/amberiv/occlusion_sensitive_cost. The video presentation can be found at https://youtu.be/8hjzrj6_2Gw.
